This study explores how opinions are shaped and social connections evolve in a complex system, governed by a delicate balance between friendly and hostile relationships. We have developed a model that captures how individuals with limited confidence in their judgments form opinions based on their personal relationships. We considered scenarios with one and two distinct aspects of opinions, and found that our framework consistently leads to the separation of agents into two distinct groups, characterized by distinct opinion sets. Depending on the level of trust, these groups either develop uniform views or multiple distinct perspectives within each group emerge. In the case of opinions based on a single dimension, the two groups have opposing views, forming a 'left' and 'right' category. In scenarios with multiple dimensions, the two groups are separated by a dividing line in opinion space. We have demonstrated that our results can partially explain a phenomenon previously observed by other researchers. Our work has implications for understanding how political ideologies become fragmented and how new parties might emerge.

We've investigated a newly constructed series of asymptotically flat, electrically charged black holes that form scalar "hair" when their charge increases at a fixed mass. Inside the event horizon, these black holes resemble a holographic superconducting material, exhibiting similar behavior in their scalar fields and culminating in a singularity that heavily depends on the black holes' parameters when the instability first arises. Additionally, we present a general theory in an appendix stating that certain types of stationary black holes with scalar "hair" cannot possess Cauchy horizons.

Different genes exhibiting similar activation patterns may show distinct mRNA expression levels at different time points due to variations in transcription duration, RNA breakdown speed, and processing rates. The impact of RNA splicing on delaying mRNA production cannot be ignored. We developed a model combining transcription dynamics and RNA accumulation to estimate the rates of transcription, RNA production lag, and RNA breakdown using sequencing data from multiple time points. The model blends a mechanistic approach with a flexible statistical method, incorporating uncertainty into the calculations through Bayesian estimation. We applied this model to ER-alpha activated cells from a breast cancer line, analyzing transcription using ChIP-Seq data and mature RNA quantities from mRNA-Seq data. The results from our optimization process show that a significant portion of genes experience a delay in mRNA production, ranging from a few minutes to several hours, due to various reasons including the length of the transcript, structural features, and slower transcription rates.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes.

Chiral SU(N) gauge theories, consisting of Weyl fermions and additional fermions, are examined to analyze their dynamics. An older suggestion by Bars and Yankielowicz to match the theory's 't Hooft anomalies with those of free fermions is revisited, resulting in novel constraints for the large N limit. Furthermore, SU(N) theories with an additional Weyl fermion are studied, demonstrating a matching of 21 't Hooft anomalies with a Spin(8) gauge theory. This discovery hints at a non-supersymmetric expansion of the Pouliot and Strassler duality, while non-supersymmetric dualities involving vector-like matter in SO(N) and Sp(N) gauge theories, subject to Weingarten inequalities, are also explored.

A linear complementary pair of group codes $(C, D)$ is formed when the direct sum of $C$ and $D$ results in the entire group algebra $R[G]$, given a finite principal ideal ring $R$ and a finite group $G$. We identify a required and confirming criterion for pairs of group codes $(C, D)$ in group algebra $R[G]$ to be a linear complementary pair, subsequently proving the equivalence in terms of permutations between codes $C$ and the dual code $D^{\perp}$.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach, to provide a substantial performance enhancement. We formally prove the correctness of our framework and, by extension, our model. Experimental results validate the significant runtime improvements yielded by our approach.

The visual appearance and auditory qualities of an object provide dual insights into its material properties.  In everyday situations, information from vision and hearing arrive simultaneously, but the integration of asynchronous cues is essential, as seen when we locate an object dropped on the ground after hearing its fall.  In this paper, a controlled environment for studying 3D object localization in real-time is established, involving an embodied robotic agent, a camera, and a microphone that identify a dropped object in a room.  The robot achieves this by synthesizing audio and visual cues along with the principles of physical mechanics governing object behavior.  A robot's efficiency in recovering dropped objects has practical significance, spanning applications from household chores to search and rescue operations.  In our experiments, we evaluated the performance of our robot under various scenarios, demonstrating its ability to adapt to unknown environments.  The developed approach is versatile, succeeding in localizing objects across a range of situations, including hidden objects, those partially obstructed, or those dropped from out-of-sight positions.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictional state transition and shear thickening phenomena. By combining micromechanical simulations with experimental verifications, scientists establish that shear thickening is a universally predictable, multifaceted process based on material properties, density, friction, and stress. Additionally, studies reveal that abrupt shear thickening is often associated with a transition to a state of rigidity, a phenomenon observable in systems ranging from simple powders to active matter, where universal patterns hold true across diverse examples.

This study investigates the fluctuating electricity consumption in Ghana's period of power shortages by applying Markov switching models, namely MS-AR and AR. The data, comprising hourly electricity usage from January 1, 2014 to December 31, 2014 provided by the Ghana Grid company, helped determine the best-fitting model as MS(2)-AR(4) based on different evaluation criteria. The parameters of this model were then estimated using an expectation-maximization algorithm, indicating that the likelihood of experiencing low electricity consumption is about 89%, with the low consumption period expected to last around 7.8 hours a day. The model outperformed traditional AR models by effectively modeling peak and varied consumption patterns and identifying distinct regime changes during the power crisis periods.

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. The study's results show that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms and the possible strategies to prevent them from overlooking essential information. Notably, our data reveal that as much as 20% of the necessary information may go undetected due to the influence of Web search personalisation. This study's findings highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, suggesting the necessity for training on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions. In addition, it is crucial that these professionals are provided with guidelines to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant information.

Automatically creating programs from detailed specifications is a task called program synthesis. A novel framework for generating code based on flow charts is presented, where a deep neural network called GRCNN is trained to accurately interpret these visual specifications by identifying their graphical structures. By being trained end-to-end, GRCNN is capable of simultaneously predicting node types, edge connections, and program order. By analyzing the binary representation of flow charts, GRCNN can learn to recognize distinct patterns associated with different conditional operation choices. The framework's results reveal strong performance advantages compared to previous methods, demonstrating substantial gains in accuracy for synthesizing programs based on flow charts.

This text explores multiple reduction techniques that facilitate the connection of Earth's climate models of varying complexity, emphasizing approaches that enable thorough reduction. It distills key mathematical concepts behind each method while showcasing several benchmark climate modeling examples for illustrative purposes.

The groundbreaking discovery of gravitational waves emanating from a binary neutron star merger in August 2017 paved the way for a new era in multimessenger astronomy. Kilonovae, produced by the expelled material from neutron star collisions, present an attractive opportunity for optical and near-infrared follow-up observations following the detection of GWs. The observation of the kilonova from GW 1780817 revealed crucial evidence for the astrophysical site of heavy element formation via the rapid neutron capture process or r-process. Given that properties of the emission are heavily influenced by the opacities of the expelled material, recent calls for enhancement in the limited available r-process atomic data have led to an increased need for precise atomic structure calculations. Consequently, this research aims to alleviate the present limitations in atomic structure data, focusing specifically on the Os-like isoelectronic sequence for low-charge ions by employing the relativistic atomic structure code for an Os IV calculation and the Ag-like isoelectronic sequence for low-charge ions by calculating the Ag IV atomic model using the relativistic atomic structure code. An Ag IV calculation was also carried out with the code. An Ag IV calculation was also carried out with the code. An Ag IV calculation was also carried out with the code.

Radiation oncologists' goal is to target tumors accurately while shielding surrounding vital organs, specifically the stomach and intestines, from x-ray beams. The incorporation of MR-Linac systems allows real-time tumor positioning, enabling precise radiation dosage adjustments based on shifting cell populations. The manual process of identifying these organs and calibrating X-ray beams can be lengthy, extending treatment times up to one hour a day, making automated techniques with deep learning essential. A recent paper explores the use of deep learning-based automation to streamline this complex task and provide faster access to treatment for a greater number of patients.

Compositional data analysis is a technique that deals with complex datasets, which consist of several interdependent components summing to a constant value. Common constant values are 1 and 100%. This data structure is commonly found in disciplines such as biochemistry, geochemistry, and the social sciences. Researchers often examine compositional data in "omics" studies with large numbers of samples. The method involves calculating logratios – the logarithmic expressions of component proportions. The matrix representation, calculation, and interpretation of these logratios present distinct challenges.

The exoplanet sample from CORALIE/HARPS (Mayor et al., 2011), which was discovered through Doppler radial velocity measurements, does not demonstrate the anticipated 'desert' at high masses (10-$100 M_\odot) with close orbital radii (<=3 AU), as predicted by the runaway gas accretion theory. Notably, similar findings have emerged from the MOA gravitational microlensing survey, which did not detect the 'desert' effect for planets in slightly longer-period orbits with lower-mass host stars (Suzuki et al., 2018). These studies collectively suggest that runaway accretion is unlikely a dominant process in shaping the final mass and orbital characteristics of exoplanets according to core accretion theory.

Artificial intelligence models, modeled after biological agents, can regulate their awareness by restricting their input from the environment to minimize information overload.  A key consideration here is, can a limited perception of its surroundings by an artificial intelligence be efficiently utilized for task accomplishment.  A new method we put forth learns control of a focused "spotlight" in the artificial intelligence by boosting its comprehension of correlations between the external world and its focus, at each step of processing.  To achieve this, an internal mental map of its condition is developed which makes predictions about where it may need more information.  A key feature of this approach is its simultaneous training of attentional focus alongside a self-modifying storage facility for observational history, enabling it to monitor unperceived surroundings and keeping track of partial data as well as the unobserved condition.  Through our work on basic reinforcement learning tasks we've found that the artificial intelligence efficiently concentrates on relevant information, efficiently utilizes its historical knowledge and effectively explores its surroundings.  A video demonstration of this behavior can be seen at: https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/simai/video/hacm/.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve complex problems that demand memory, error correction, and selection capabilities, mirroring brain circuit behaviors, albeit with limited applicability due to large training demands and memory needs. Brain structures pose constraints such as synaptic distance costs and thus inspired local masking, allowing task-independent predetermined graphs, even with sparsity levels as low as 4\%. We introduce locality-masked RNNs and make several breakthroughs, demonstrating these models match or outperform traditional fully-connected RNNs without manual network construction, can learn and adapt faster while reducing the data required to perform cognitive tasks efficiently. Additionally, we developed Mod-Cog, a comprehensive set of cognitive tasks which bridges simple learning tasks and more complex real-world brain challenges, providing robust experimentation to compare different network architectures and support artificial general intelligence research, while also creating SpaNet, a 12- neuron sparse network outperforming traditional RNNs on 11 tasks in our benchmark.

We categorize nilpotent algebras by dimension with a focus on their commutative, commutative nilpotent and anticommutative properties. Our findings reveal the irreducibility of corresponding geometric spaces, allowing us to accurately calculate their dimensions and establish general families of algebras associated with each space. Additionally, we demonstrate how these results contribute to an understanding of the length of anticommutative algebras in further study.

Active galactic nuclei with exceptionally powerful radio signals are among the brightest known celestial sources, spanning across a wide range of wavelengths. These powerful jets from supermassive black holes can significantly influence both the black hole's growth and its surroundings in the vast expanse of space. In the radio spectrum, these jets can be observed on various scales, but their X-ray and gamma-ray emissions are predicted to be concentrated on smaller scales, typically under 10 parsecs. Recent findings by the Chandra X-ray telescope have revealed the presence of kiloparsec-scale jets, which has sparked debate about the source of their high-energy radiation. Understanding the origins of this high-energy radiation is essential for clarifying how these large-scale jets interact with their surroundings. In this investigation, we explore the potential for large-scale jets to be compressed by massive radio signals, such as radio beams, which can lead to the generation of X-rays and gamma-rays through shock formation. This model predicts that in the vicinity of AGNs, dense plasma is generated by large-scale jets being compressed by radio signals, resulting in the production of observable X-rays and gamma-rays. This process not only affects the jet but also impacts the growth of the supermassive black hole, with implications that extend to the cosmic web in the vast expanse of space. In this study, we examine how this mechanism influences the evolution of AGNs and their jets at the highest redshifts, focusing on their potential detectability through observations of cosmic microwave background

We perform a covariant expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action in powers of
$1/c^2$, considering a generic spacetime foliation defined by $c$, the speed
of light. We achieve this through the application of a suitable 'pre-non-
relativistic' geometrical parametrization, thereby facilitating an
analytical $1/c^2$ expansion of general relativity. Ultimately, this method
permits an in-depth examination of the Einstein-Hilbert action expansion up to
its next-to-next-to-leading order.

This study presents an enhanced approach to 3D image features that incorporates invariance to discrete symmetry by considering inversions of spatial axes and image contrast.  The proposed descriptor includes a binary feature that distinguishes between the sign of the Laplacian operator's results applied to image data and reversed contrast, resulting in a total of four possible states.  Combining this with the extension of the Symmetric-Improved Approximate Nearest Neighbor (S-IANN) matching algorithm for multi-state feature comparisons, we develop a new point-to-point partial registration method for three-dimensional images.  Our method, specifically designed for medical imaging applications, utilizes two libraries of image features derived from two inputs: one extracted from scanned image data and the other from scanned anatomy, both pre-processed to remove redundant information.  By applying a symmetric distance measure, we evaluate the similarity between all feature pairs, and those with suitable ratios of similar states are grouped and used to define partial registration outcomes.  Our method, which runs efficiently due to its sparse data processing, does not require further refinement with optimization algorithms.  As evidence of its effectiveness, we demonstrate its application in registering cerebral cortex images, detecting anomalies in CT scans, and identifying abnormalities in MRI lung disease images.

We've analyzed the data from a unique binary star system, SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, based on our comprehensive photometry observations taken over 318 days. These observations revealed detailed insights into the binary's behavior and allowed us to refine the time of the mid-eclipse. Using individual filter light curve fittings, we determined the low-mass star components and companion star sizes of the binary, finding the white dwarf has a radius of 0.031 R sun, while its companion has a radius of 0.013 R sun at an angle of 87.7 degrees. Furthermore, based on our most suitable model, we estimated the system's total mass as approximately 0.88 M sun. Light curve modeling also showed that the binary's smaller star is situated at the center of the system, surrounded by extensive circumbinary material with an outer edge at around 2.8 magnetic radii from the white dwarf. Based on our most suitable model, we estimated the secondary star's oblateness ratio as approximately 0.16. Additionally, using various data, we estimated the system's distance as around 811 parsecs based on the white dwarf mass.

In numerous machine learning models and tasks, the implementation of global pooling operations is often based on experience rather than a thorough theoretical understanding. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that most current global pooling methods are essentially specialized solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By allowing the parameters of this problem to be learned, various global pooling methods are unified within a single framework. Consequently, a generalized global pooling layer for neural networks called UOT-Pooling (UOTP) has been proposed. To implement this UOTP layer, the classic Sinkhorn-scaling algorithm is employed. Furthermore, a new model architecture based on the Bregman ADMM algorithm is designed, which offers better numerical stability and improved ability to reproduce existing pooling layers. The proposed UOTP layers are then tested across several applications, including multi-instance learning, graph classification, and image classification, and are found to be capable of either mimicking conventional global pooling layers or developing novel, performance-enhancing pooling mechanisms.

The primary objective of this research is to examine aspects of the validity of the active galactic nucleus unification theory through comparing the characteristics of radio-quiet and radio-loud active galactic nuclei. By leveraging a comprehensive sample of 332 AGN spanning radio-quiet to radio-loud spectrums, our analysis focuses on the distribution of galaxy type, axis ratio, and position angle. Our data set consists of piecemeal information gathered from various references, which we consolidated into a database. In contrast to previous studies, our results indicate that radio-quiet and radio-loud AGN differ significantly in terms of galaxy type, with the latter being more prevalent in larger, more massive hosts. Moreover, our data suggest that the distribution of narrow-line region depth also varies according to radio luminosity, with wider line-emitting regions associated with radio-loud sources. Additionally, we discovered subtle differences in the distribution of host galaxy ellipticity and the mean position angle among our sample AGN. We propose that the growth of supermassive black holes in radio-loud sources is accelerated by energetic jets that stimulate the merger-driven star formation that feeds the black hole, resulting in larger, more massive hosts. In contrast, radio-quiet AGN, which tend to reside in smaller, less massive hosts, are thought to acquire their fuel through smooth accretion.

This paper delves into a comprehensive analysis of general rotational surfaces in the 4-dimensional Euclidean space, focusing on flat general rotation surfaces characterized by a 1-type Gauss map. Additionally, it's established that a non-planar, flat general rotation surface with this distinct Gauss map is a Lie group if and only if it's a Clifford torus.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification for pre-training, a method which can
be marred by unrepresentative training sets. On the other hand, depth estimation,
a fully supervised task, might offer a more inclusive starting point with better
generalizability. In this research, we investigate and demonstrate the
effectiveness of utilizing depth estimation for pre-training semantic segmentation
models, particularly in scenarios involving limited annotated samples. Our
results show that models trained on publicly available depth estimation and PASCAL
Plus+ datasets prior to PASCAL VOC 2012 can achieve higher mIoU scores, 5.8%
and 2.2% greater respectively, than those trained on ImageNet for pre-training. 
Additionally, we find that models pre-trained on depth estimation exhibit greater
robustness to perturbations in the input.

This work introduces TCube, a novel GPT-3 powered system that generates
narratives for time-series data, explaining complex trends and patterns in a
transparent way. TCube uses a neural model as its language model partner to
augment GPT-3's capabilities, particularly in domains where it lacks expertise.
By integrating the neural model, TCube enhances its story-telling abilities,
making it more versatile and efficient. For instance, TCube can analyze sales
data and identify key moments or compare branching options in decision-making
processes, all while maintaining transparency.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$.
On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation.

This study explores the well-posedness of global solutions, dependence on initial data, and potential loss of regularity in strictly hyperbolic equations with certain properties. These equations feature coefficients that experience moderate blow-up as sublogarithmic growth, represented by the function $|\ln t|^\gamma$ where $0 < \gamma < 1$. By applying a specific metric on the phase space, we can categorize these equations and examine their coefficients, which have polynomial bounds in x, x-derivatives, and a specific rate of decrease in t. We leverage a Planck function, based on this metric, to split the phase space and define relevant generalized symbol classes. Through the use of a conjugating pseudodifferential operator, which we term the loss operator, we establish an energy estimate and identify a link between the loss of regularity and the phase space metric, thus making the loss operator a $H^\ell$ operator. Consequently, we prove the global well-posedness of these equations and the nature of the loss of regularity, which we illustrate through examples.

This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese word segmentation. Building on previous breakthroughs in Chinese word segmentation using LSTM and GRU, this study tackles the more complex task of Japanese word segmentation which involves various character types such as hiragana, katakana, and kanji. These characters lead to significant orthographic variations making Japanese word segmentation particularly demanding. To address this issue, this study proposes an LSTM-based model for Japanese word segmentation, taking into consideration the essential global context. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed model attains exceptional accuracy when evaluated across different Japanese corpora.

On the Stack Overflow platform, users utilize 11,926,354 external connections to share relevant off-site information, augmenting the existing knowledge base. This collaborative effort involves repeated link sharing activities, where 82.5% of all links are external and 57.0% consist of frequently shared resources. To streamline users' knowledge management, this study delves into the characteristics of these shared links to identify common patterns in external resources that are repeatedly disseminated. Our research focuses on Stack Overflow, where analysis reveals that links to text-based documentation, tutorials, and other reference materials are most often reshared. This leads to observations regarding the reasons for link sharing, including the promotion of individual profiles, the dissemination of educational resources, and the promotion of one's own work. This findings are further substantiated by surveys, revealing that users employ link sharing to various ends, and users largely agree that these links enhance the quality of Stack Overflow content. Nevertheless, some users feel that these links dilute the discussion or are irrelevant, highlighting potential areas for improvement in the future development of external collaboration tools on Stack Overflow.

Galactic diversity is addressed by investigating the variability of galaxies across different periods and sizes, and determining whether observed differences are solely attributed to a galaxy's stage of development. Analysis of a comprehensive galaxy database reveals that a significant portion of galaxies exhibit variability, and the relationship between a galaxy's size and optical variability intensities is complex. However, it has been discovered that a large number of galaxies with varying sizes and stages of development share similar properties and characteristics among themselves, and therefore, require an explanation beyond what can be attributed to their distinct developmental stages.

Although climate change is widely accepted, meaningful conversations about it are scarce,
resulting in slow implementation of the necessary societal changes to mitigate its effects.
To enhance climate communication and promote individual actions, we are developing a system
that leverages climate information tailored to each person's values. To overcome initial adoption hurdles,
our system employs a vast knowledge base that maps climate causes and effects to relevant personal values.
Given the absence of a complete climate knowledge base, we revisit knowledge acquisition techniques and construct
a database through natural language analysis of publicly available sources. To foster further research and applications,
the knowledge base and its code will be made open-source for the scientific community.

Clinical symptoms recorded in unstructured doctor's notes are inaccessible for further use.
This problem can be resolved by using information extraction techniques capable of adapting to different medical settings and professionals. 
In this research, we address the issue of extracting symptoms by using pre-trained and fine-tuned models, trained on diverse patient data, medical institutions, and specialties. 
To reduce dependency on specific data, we develop an adaptive strategy for extracting symptoms by temporarily removing commonly mentioned symptoms from the original data source. 
This approach employs pre-trained vectors to measure similarity between the source and target environments, and then uses the similarity to determine the appropriate number of symptoms to forget. 
By forgetting irrelevant symptoms, the model is able to focus on essential ones and achieve better adaptation to new, unseen settings. 
Experiments using this strategy showed positive results on extracting symptoms in three specific areas with high precision and accuracy.

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm that enables autonomous systems to learn and adapt through trial and error, ultimately leading to optimal performance. Despite initial challenges associated with learning direct policies, deep reinforcement learning has overcome this obstacle, paving the way for widespread application in industries such as transportation. A simulated driving environment serves as the primary locus for deep reinforcement learning training, where numerous tasks can be concurrently learned or sequentially targeted. This document outlines a comprehensive framework for deep reinforcement learning in driving, assuming a lack of existing background knowledge.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks. This model's parameters can be efficiently initialised based on the principles of statistical independence, leading to significant reductions in the number of parameters. Extensive simulations with datasets of varying sizes have shown that this Random Neural Network accurately classifies images, reaches a spike frequency similar to that of the original neural network, and at the same time substantially decreases the network's complexity and energy consumption.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields.

A surge in personal device ownership offers an immense, yet largely underutilized resource of computational power, making it feasible to utilize it. To harness this potential, we developed Pando, a novel volunteer computing system based on declarative concurrent programming, and powered by JavaScript, WebRTC, and WebSockets. By employing a dynamic network of unreliable, volunteer-sourced personal devices and their browsers, Pando facilitates parallel execution of a function on multiple values, thus enhancing efficiency on compute-intensive applications like animation rendering and image processing. Furthermore, our approach's adaptability is demonstrated through Pando's deployment across a range of platforms, encompassing local networks, Grid5000, and PlanetLab's distributed nodes spanning across Europe.

A computational method for resolving nonlinear eigenvalue problems is presented, using an approximating function derived from the eigenvalues of a modified problem.  By employing a variable sampling process that focuses data collection on the areas most critical to solution resolution, this algorithm efficiently distributes resources. It then uses the collected information to produce approximations for the sought-after eigenvalues and eigenvectors through further processing. Several numerical demonstrations highlight the performance of this solution strategy.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. By employing this equivalence, we obtain a detailed characterization of these transformations, yielding new insights and results in various areas, such as Krieger embeddings, survivor sets, Hausdorff dimensions, bifurcation sets, and badly approximable numbers. We show that certain classes of sets associated with these beta-transformations possess unique properties, specifically that they are winning in Schmidt games and have the countable intersection property.

We've found that gauge theories with $SO(N_{c})$ as a gauge group and matter fields represented as vectors confine, resulting from monopole condensation and the quark bilinear breaking $SU(N_{F})$ chiral symmetry down to $SO(N_{F})$. Our findings derive from an ${\cal N}=1$ supersymmetric theory, specifically with anomaly-mediated supersymmetry breaking.

Machine learning models such as random forests and AdaBoost have proven effective across many fields but their high performance comes at the cost of clarity in understanding their predictions. Users are generally unable to discern how individual characteristics, or sets of characteristics, influence these models as their values change. In order to improve this understanding, a method called Disentangled Attribution Curves has been introduced to offer more transparent explanations for tree ensemble models through detailed (multi-dimensional) curves depicting feature importance at different variable values. By using this new approach, it is possible to boost the accuracy of regression models and maintain clarity, even on complex datasets. An in-depth analysis is provided through the examination of predictive errors, as well as a practical example, to demonstrate the benefits of Disentangled Attribution Curves. Furthermore, a publicly available R package offers easy access to using this new approach in practical applications.

In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them unsuitable for practical application. This work presents an alternative solution by harnessing the capabilities of Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard data, offering a more efficient approach to collaborative machine learning. We propose an efficient framework, Flatee, allowing parties to train models while preserving confidentiality, utilizing techniques like Secure Multi-Party Computation and Homomorphic Encryption in conjunction with CELOS, a vectorized evaluation protocol facilitating faster processing within a Trusted Execution Environment. By integrating these components, Flatee provides a substantial performance improvement over existing methods, bringing the realm of efficient collaboration closer to reality.

The embedded systems industry is massive and ubiquitous, as evidenced by its presence in most of the world's produced processors. Interactions between drivers and external components like sensors and actuators pose significant challenges to embedded software development, particularly during the testing phase. Factors such as environmental unpredictability, limited hardware availability, and costs often hinder effective testing. To address these issues, this research introduces a novel testing framework that targets driver verification on microcontrollers. It comprises a simulated external environment, a temporary validation setup, and a tool that generates and runs tests. To illustrate its utility, the framework is applied to validate the I2C driver in the Zephyr operating system.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system.

Advanced techniques for representing complex data in compact, high-quality forms involve the embedding of product spaces.
We've identified a new challenge - linear classification in complex product space structures composed of different geometric environments, like Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic spaces.
To tackle this problem, we develop a groundbreaking approach for projecting complex data into a unified, geometric space that maintains its original structural attributes.
We demonstrate that any linear classification task in such complex environments can be simplified to a similar task within a transformed space with tailored linear constraints.
Our proposed method offers flexible adaptations to various geometric environments and can be optimized for specific data distributions through hyperparameter adjustments.
Ultimately, we show that this method excels over existing product space classification methods and competitive baselines, achieving substantial improvements of up to 30% in accuracy, particularly for data with imbalanced classes.

This introduction focuses on stochastic Model Predictive Control methods that account for uncertainty in constraints, illustrated through a linear system under unpredictable conditions. The corresponding Matlab code is also accessible online for reference purposes.

This paper bridges the gap between compressed sensing and statistical learning, leveraging sparsity and structure to minimize the computational burden of learning tasks. We focus on independent component analysis through a compressive lens, demonstrating that certain properties within the cumulant-based ICA model yield a compact set of solutions that can be encompassed by a lower-dimensional manifold. An efficient algorithm is developed to accurately determine the manifold's positioning, which effectively reduces dimensionality. Notably, the compressive ICA problem is found to have an optimal solution given constrained measurements, achieving a form of duality between the two. An alternative, flexible cumulant-based model is introduced for higher-order sources, which incorporates a parameterized frequency domain approach. An iterative algorithm, akin to expectation-maximization, is developed using the flexible model through emulating the compressive ICA problem's duality. The novel algorithms are tested using synthetic data and compared against conventional ICA methods, with successful applications to relevant fields like spectroscopy and neuroimaging.

To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusion of one species, distinct population coexistence, or bistable coexistence dependent on the model's parameter settings. The model shows a critical transition from a monostable to a bistable state as the noise level exceeds a certain threshold, with increasing noise levels also affecting the exclusion of one species. The model's results show a critical role of lattice regularity in these outcomes, as well as the impact of species dispersal differences on their competitive relationships.
We prove that von Neumann algebras associated with compact regions within abelian quantum double models have infinite type $II$.

To enhance magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in cavity magnomechanics, we develop an approach incorporating a coherent feedback loop. Furthermore, our findings confirm that both the steady and dynamic states exhibit genuine tripartite entanglement. We utilize the logarithmic negativity to quantify quantum correlations between individual subsystems, as well as genuine tripartite entanglement via the condition for existence in the steady state. We leverage the influence of the feedback strength and intracavity frequencies to adjust entanglement among tripartite, bipartite photon, magnon, and phonon systems. We identify that the magnon-photon sector exhibits the greatest quantum correlation, whereas the phonon-photon sector shows the least. Moreover, the tripartite entanglement is prominent over the bipartite phonon-photon one. Our entanglement analysis offers valuable insights into the design of cavity magnomechanics for tripartite entanglement of magnons, photons, and phonons.

We've obtained one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for color and spin spaces, applicable to all five scenarios: $q \to qq'\bar{q}'$, $q \to qq\bar{q}$, $q \to qgg$, $g \to gq\bar{q}$ and $g \to ggg$. The exact expressions are derived within dimensionless QCD and include the results of a specific integral up to its second-order expansion. Additionally, we've evaluated the associated splitting functions. Our results are crucial and serve as a necessary foundation for developing theoretical cross-sections at the one-loop level.

A formal proof for the Neron Desingularization, a multidimensional case algorithm, has been formulated and applied to one-dimensional local rings, and this concept is currently being used within Singular software implementation. Furthermore, a relevant theorem based on Greenberg's Strong Approximation theorem has also been introduced and applied to the realm of one-dimensional local rings.

Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with the classical Islamic civilization utilizing the Sun's daily movement to determine prayer times, often relying on sundials for this purpose. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a reflection of local advancements in astronomy, technology, art, and architecture, with historical examples warranting detailed documentation and study, though often overlooked in existing literature. To collect necessary spatial and temporal information on these sundials, a citizen science initiative could be implemented, addressing research inquiries while promoting science education and empowering local communities to preserve their historical heritage. This concept has been proposed as a framework, referred to as the Suryakala-Nusantara program, to explore sundials through citizen science methods.

This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data to those in need and supply power to those who require it. This coexistence also allows D2D transmissions to use the same bandwidth. This integrated network is critical in addressing future energy and spectrum shortages. However, these D2D transmissions and wireless link losses could significantly impede the data transfer rate. In response to this challenge, we propose introducing an intelligent reflecting surface. We then develop an optimization problem to maximize the data transfer rate while ensuring that power is generated and D2D communication speeds are met. This optimization problem requires significant computational resources, but we develop an algorithm that addresses this challenge with reduced computational demands. Finally, simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

The surge in telework needs has highlighted the potential benefits of fully
automating and controlling experiments remotely. This work presents the technical
advancements of creating a two-dimensional LDV measurement system using a single-
point LDV system via a remotely controllable and automated setup. The document's
aim is to expedite the development of similar setups for this kind of application,
which is highly versatile and can be applied to various scenarios including both
air-based acoustic signal-driven samples and mechanically induced samples.

The cardinalities of finite models for sentences with at least three variables and binary relations are examined in this study.  Specifically, we demonstrate that any such sentence, denoted as $\Phi$, has a corresponding sentence, denoted as $\Phi'$, utilizing the same number of variables and one symmetric binary relation, whose set of model cardinalities increases linearly with $\Phi$'s model cardinalities. Furthermore, we observe that the models of sentence $\Phi'$ are all bipartite graph representations.  Consequently, we deduce that, in order to resolve Asser's conjecture regarding the class's closure under complement, we may focus solely on examining sentences with at most three variables whose models consist of undirected bipartite graphs.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 5 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our research implies that a programmable phase plate 
can successfully compensate for spherical aberration, though design constraints may 
limit its suitability for certain applications.

Drawing inspiration from Feynman's and Deutsch's groundbreaking work, we introduce a theoretical framework that assesses computational capability across diverse physical platforms and complexity scales. This framework is utilized to analyze the fundamental principles of quantum computation. Furthermore, this study serves as a precursor to investigating more universal computation models by examining additional physical mechanisms exemplified throughout the paper.

This study focused on determining the general equation for calculating the potential positions of an $n$ step random walk in a $d$ dimensional space with a single unit step size, denoted as $|P_n^{d}|$. Our approach began by establishing a recursive relationship for the count formula: $|P_n^{d+1}| = |P_n^d| + 2\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} |P_k^d|$. We then presented two distinct methods to derive an explicit equation for $|P_n^{d}|$, involving the application of generating functions and Faulhaber's formula. Ultimately, our findings were presented in a matrix representation as our primary theorem.

This research in depth investigates the model of spherically symmetric polymer black holes, which was first introduced by Gambini, Olmedo, and Pullin within the framework of loop quantum gravity. We explored how in the GOP model the spacelike transition surface at the classical singularity replaces it. Utilizing transformations in the coordinates, the authors were able to extend the metric to the white hole region, which led to discovering that the structure of the quantum black hole mirrors that of its classical counterpart during both phases of the process. Moreover, the authors found that just as in the classical case, the horizons' radii are directly proportional to the mass parameter. Leveraging the techniques of Green's function and scattering theory, the authors were able to derive a formula for quasinormal frequencies of perturbed black holes. The analysis of the quasinormal spectrum as the detuning parameter is adjusted indicates that the negative quasinormal frequencies are not unique to the polymer black hole, but rather they are a characteristic of the spacetime structure itself. Additionally, the authors discovered that the real part of the quasinormal frequencies is proportional to the detuning parameter, which led to calculating the corresponding imaginary part.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which exhibits both a plasma-like response at low frequencies and a pie-like shape at higher frequencies. This correlation is used to calculate the dynamic charge susceptibility of doped graphene. The obtained results are in good agreement with a recent finite-temperature quantum Monte Carlo study. Furthermore, using the RPA approximation, we have developed a finite-temperature theory for determining the contribution of long-range interactions to the heat capacity of doped graphene, which is an essential requirement for future high-precision heat capacity measurements on graphene.

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context information during synthesis. A new framework, masked speech synthesis, incorporates a context masking module that leverages neural networks to select and intensify relevant contextual features from a prior speech segment. These selected features enhance the current speech segment's acoustic characteristics, improving model coherence. Additionally, the framework includes a mask generation module that predicts optimal masking patterns for enhanced results. By integrating masked speech features into current speech segments, the synthesis process yields more coherent speech samples. Experimental evaluations on the VIVOSpeech corpus demonstrate that our proposed framework surpasses the performance of baseline models and a previously developed context-aware speech synthesis system.

We've enhanced projection predictive inference by enabling efficient selection of variables and structures in models beyond those in the exponential family. By projecting predictive variables into a latent space, we have created a generalized framework that: 1) maintains the original model's integrity while performing variable selection, 2) accurately detects relevant structures and retains posterior uncertainties, and 3) extends its applicability to non-Gaussian models within the exponential family. We've rigorously evaluated our approach by comparing it with established methods on various datasets, and the results demonstrate its superior performance.

Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to strategically crafted malicious inputs, prompting the development of countermeasures against query-optimization attacks. Our research diverges from previous studies by exploring the vulnerability of DNN models to Man-in-the-Middle attacks. From an attacker's standpoint, conventional adversarial attacks prove ineffective as they necessitate multiple interactions with the model prior to execution, whereas MitM attacks can launch without this limitation. Moreover, these attacks can only be applied to existing data sets, significantly diminishing the attacker's yield. Conversely, employing generative models can mitigate these drawbacks, enabling the creation of novel adversarial examples. Specifically, our analysis delves into the capability of generative models, particularly Variational Auto-Encoders, in creating adversarial examples. Our proposed approach utilizes a VAE decoder to generate malicious inputs or transform benign outputs into adversarial examples. Our results show that our method enables successful MitM attacks on both MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets at an impressive rate, rivaling the effectiveness of existing query-optimization attacks. Moreover, our approach boasts considerable efficiency, executing 104 times faster than state-of-the-art query-optimization attacks.

Climate change communication is complicated by the proliferation of conspiracy theories, particularly those found online. This research investigates prevalent conspiracy theories regarding climate change by analyzing a significant Twitter dataset and applies a sophisticated stance detection technique. Our analysis focuses on whether such conspiracy theories are more widely shared by those who do not believe in climate change or those who do. Furthermore, we examine the most popular conspiracy theories, their variations with differing levels of climate change acceptance, and reveal that non-believers predominantly disseminate messages containing conspiracy theory-related keywords. Notably, all conspiracy theories are not equally prevalent. Our findings also highlight their implications for effective climate change communication strategies.

A study focused on the production of dark matter in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV has been carried out using a dataset with 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of data that was recorded by the CMS experiment. This study examined single top quark and top quark pair events combined, focusing on the final states with one or two isolated muons, and considered the case where no isolation was applied to the leading muon. By utilizing techniques such as likelihood ratio tests, comparisons between data and predicted backgrounds were made across various dark matter mass and spin-to-mass ratio scenarios. This study did not reveal any significant findings beyond expectations, and thus established new, stringent lower limits on the cross-sectional values for certain dark matter production scenarios, with the limits ranging from 0.08 to 0.70 fb in different scenarios, with the limits being most stringent when the dark matter mass was around 30-100 GeV.

Given an n-exangulated category with specified properties, we establish that it satisfies Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality if and only if it possesses certain duality-based angles. We also determine a specific condition necessary for the presence of Serre duality. Assuming duality exists, we establish a one-to-one correspondence involving a bijection and specific category characteristics.

Building upon Kirkeboen et al.'s (2016) work, we explore the potential of ranking theory in the context of unordered treatments in the context of return on education investment. The application of this approach yields a straightforward CV criterion that facilitates the identification of the most effective treatment without necessitating the creation of a synthetic control or an instrumental variable with a ordered outcome. Using data from Norway, we discover that returning to field of study provides a more accurate prediction of the return on investment than the conventional method, with the difference being substantial enough to influence policy decisions.

To advance our understanding of matter's various forms, high-energy particle collisions with a wide variety of projectiles must be studied extensively.
Although scientists have utilized beams of numerous particles to make significant breakthroughs, creating and working with beams of antineutrons, specific hyperons and their counterparts has been notoriously challenging.
However, a recent high-tech research setup known as a super $J/\psi$ factory holds the potential to greatly improve access to these elusive particles. As a result, a huge number of $J/\psi$ decays occur annually, creating favorable conditions for accurately measuring minute differences in cross-sectional frequencies based on isospin, parity and other physical characteristics.
This potential has prompted us to calculate the production yields of a huge number of hyperons and their counterparts when collided with a stationary target, utilizing state-of-the-art software. Our estimates include not only traditionally hard-to-create states but also a wide range of more accessible reactions, such as the $J/\psi$ energy-dependent selection, a vast production of $\Lambda$ (144 times more than the current largest machine's potential) and other antiparticles, which could lead to significant breakthroughs in physics.

Most of a multiple star system's final mass is accumulated during the first few million years of its existence, specifically during the protostellar and protoplanetary phases.  Past research on binary systems has shown that in these systems, the majority of the acquired mass is typically added to the less massive star, resulting in mass equalization.  Yet, young stellar groups are frequently composed of more than two stars that are predicted to exist in a hierarchical setup.  Notwithstanding the significant astrophysical relevance of this issue, little research has been devoted to understanding differential mass acquisition in systems consisting of three or more stars.  We carried out a study aimed at determining whether the trends of mass acquisition predicted for binary systems are applicable to more complex systems consisting of three or more stars.  Utilizing three-dimensional Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics simulations, our research team used the code Phantom to model the growth of both equal-mass and unequal-mass stars within hierarchical triple systems consisting of a protostar and two points of mass loss.  Our results show the less massive star in each system acquires the majority of its final mass through a process involving it being closer to the point of mass loss.  We also discovered that in systems with equal-mass stars, mass transfer to the less massive star varies based on the characteristics of the system, specifically the eccentricity of its orbits and the distance between the third component and the less massive star, resulting in uneven mass acquisition. This manuscript examines flat spacetimes with intrinsic properties, as viable models for understanding the universe on a cosmological scale. We find that such spacetimes naturally incorporate geometric patterns suitable for describing irregular, periodically-distributed matter within the universe. We also establish mathematical proofs for their local representation, as well as the existence and uniqueness of the Einstein's equations under these specific spatial constraints. Notably, our research uncovers an interesting set of precise solutions, illustrating how these spacetimes can be used in cosmology to model a universe transitioning from homogenous, isotropic states in the early stages to more complex distributions with voids and matter peaks over time.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The first stage of the proposed model utilizes the variational image restoration model to obtain clean image labels for a subsequent segmentation task. The second phase treats the label calculation as a standard image segmentation problem, employing the Mumford-Shah model, enhanced by a data-driven term that incorporates the restored clean labels. To efficiently solve these challenging nonlinear problems, we employ the alternating direction method of multi-pliers and the semi-implicit Euler method. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, two sets of experimental data are conducted, using real-world images of buildings and vegetables. The results demonstrate the capability of the model to accurately segment images with challenging backgrounds and diverse textures, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the relationship between the masses of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles, closing a gap in parameter space around $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Additionally, we determine the upper limits on the decay constant of axions, assuming their decay could prevent their entry into a state of instability and their possible non-observation through superradiance. This research also provides upper limits on the fraction of dark matter comprised by ultra-light axion-like particles, concluding that, as a single species, such a particle cannot constitute more than 10% of the dark matter in a given mass range ($10^{-21} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$).

Creating intelligent, neuroinspired systems poses a significant challenge due to its underlying hardware complexities. To overcome these challenges, a thorough comprehension of its fundamental building blocks is essential, coupled with innovative computational methods. To address this issue, an integrated framework has been developed, comprising a comprehensive library and a high-level simulator. The library compiles the results of theoretical computations into a manageable format, while the simulator utilizes this library to emulate neural network behavior over various system architectures. Specifically, this framework pairs the Brian simulator with the Loihi chip, providing a versatile tool for simulating neural network dynamics in both software and hardware environments.

A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from active regions experiencing significant changes in their magnetic field configurations. These storms exhibit significant intensity fluctuations in very short time frames and on very short wavelengths. The dynamic evolution of these storm sources remains largely unstudied due to a lack of high-resolution imaging data in the microwave range. We conducted a detailed analysis of a rare, extremely intense storm on AR12470 on July 13, 2021, captured by the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA), which provided high-resolution images of active region dynamics. The data showed two distinct storm sources within the active region: one in the core and the other located off-center. The storm sources demonstrated complex evolution, with visible particle beam acceleration, and the active region undergoing a significant, fine-scale magnetic disturbance. The data also showed how the storm sources change in response to a tiny microflare that produces a small but visible microwave brightening. The storm sources exhibit a previously unseen pattern of dynamic evolution, which suggests that the active region's magnetic field is reconfiguring on very short wavelengths during a small flare. The storm sources show a brief, highly correlated period of change in frequency and brightness, which suggests a complex and dynamic evolution of the active region's magnetic field.

A compact magneto-optical trap has been successfully developed, using a planar-integrated design that merges an optical grating chip and a magnetic coil chip. This novel setup minimizes the size and weight of the trap, requiring only a single laser beam to capture a population of approximately 10,000 cold rubidium atoms. The improved MOT architecture has potential applications in devices such as gravimeters, atomic clocks, and quantum memory systems, offering a reduction in volume, weight, and complexity.

The spherically symmetric merging of a kinetic cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Unlike earlier research, which established boundary conditions at a distant point, we examine this process with properties of the cloud specified within a finite sphere of radius. We use a series of models, ranging from simple to complex, to compute steady-state solutions, from a cold gas to a gas in thermal equilibrium, using various potential types. We particularly focus on the impact of angular momentum in two scenarios: a cloud with zero angular momentum and an angular momentum-specified cloud with a radial velocity distribution. We find, for all models, that a transition occurs from an accretion mode to a jet mode at a certain critical mass, influenced by factors such as potential type, boundary conditions, and thermal equilibrium. In contrast, the mass at which this transition occurs increases with the average angular momentum of the cloud in models involving a Faller potential. This research addresses questions about the formation of jets and active galactic nuclei through the merging of rotating gas clouds.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror.

A longstanding debate revolved around the origin of a rarest type of stellar outburst called a Soft X-ray Line Diversion (SXLD). There have been two primary theories: one suggests that these outbursts are triggered by the explosion of a high-mass star, specifically a Luminous Blue Variable (LBV), while another points to the explosion as a supernova ejecta interacting with the interstellar medium. Our investigation of the massive star system surrounding the young cluster Westerlund 2 revealed five LBV candidates located in the vicinity of the cluster. Following the discovery of these LBVs, we observed one of them, Westerlund 2 LBV 1, experiencing an outburst. Through the analysis of archival data and temporal observations of the outbreak, we conclude that the LBV cannot be attributed to a newly discovered SXLD or a confirmed supernova ejecta explosion. However, its orbit around the proposed binary companion appears to bring it close enough to the companion to induce mass transference, resulting in fluctuations in the mass transfer frequency. It is during one of these close approaches that Westerlund 2 LBV 1 likely experienced the outbreak.

Degraded handwritten documents, which are susceptible to damage from paper ageing and environmental factors, can cause severe readability issues for current text recognition algorithms. To overcome these challenges, we propose an innovative, end-to-end approach utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks that not only restores visual clarity but also improves the overall readability of the documents. This pioneering method differs from conventional binarization techniques, which primarily focus on enhancing visual quality, by integrating a text recognition module to optimize generated output. The effectiveness of this architecture was validated through comprehensive experiments conducted on Arabic and Latin handwritten texts, showcasing improved readability and visual quality. Additionally, our pre-trained model demonstrated exceptional performance on the H-DIBCO challenges, even after fine-tuning on synthetic, degraded text images.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such account-related fraud, a system was devised which employs ID card extraction via OCR and NLP for verification purposes.  Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables conversion of images to text, can also be used to convert an Indonesian ID card or KTP image to text.  This would facilitate easier data entry for service operators.  However, to enhance accuracy, manual correction is often required.  To simplify this process, a previous study developed a system that could extract KTP data via OCR and NLP.  This study builds upon that research by refining the existing system using machine learning techniques.  Notably, we compared several machine learning algorithms including Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, K-Nearest Neighbors, decision tree, and others, ultimately using a combination of features and algorithms to create a highly accurate extraction system.  This system surpassed the accuracy of the original study and is now being used to extract KTP data with high precision.

In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline, particularly in high-speed scenarios. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored deep learning (DL) techniques for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. Nonetheless, these approaches either underperform in extremely high-speed situations or exhibit substantial computational complexities. To resolve these issues, this paper introduces an innovative solution based on an LSTM-DL approach, aiming to enhance estimation quality, reduce computational demands, and outperform existing methods. The proposed estimator's effectiveness was confirmed through simulations conducted in Rayleigh-fading environments with two antenna configurations.

The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its subjectiveness and the immense possibilities of color combinations. In this research, a novel, semi-supervised colorization approach is proposed, allowing pre-trained models to automatically label images with the dominant color in underprocessed data. A model pre-trained on a large dataset of unmarked images can then fine-tune on a small set of marked images to generate detailed, human-generated-like colorizations for astronomical images. Additionally, a neural network-based upscaler for images was developed using a larger dataset of scaled images, outperforming competing methods in restoring both sharp and blurry images.

We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Network (ANN) weights without relying on tedious iterative processes. Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our proposed algorithm rapidly achieves low error rates in the regression and classification of intricate datasets, such as the Griewank function and the MNIST database for handwritten digits. Its mathematical formulation allows it to accurately approximate highly complex nonlinear functions with a minimal margin of error, and it also facilitates the solution of Partial Differential Equations. The rapid weight calculation capability of this method makes it notably suitable for complex problem-solving tasks that were previously thought to be intractable.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel started representing the interests of young researchers within the ECFA community in January 2021. Throughout its first two years of operation, the panel developed its organizational framework, cooperated with ECFA by offering input and insights, and introduced several projects focused on comprehending and addressing the varied needs of young researchers. This report outlines the details of the panel's formation and operations as well as its engagement with numerous activities during its first two years of operation.

Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously analyzed line waves in theory and in practice, revealing their occurrence at both microwave and terahertz frequencies.
It has also been demonstrated that these waves can occur when there's a sudden change from a negative to a positive symmetric resistance and uniform surface reactance present.
Characteristics of line waves include highly confineable mode propagation, polarization dependent on direction, and unique localized field enhancements.
A new study proposes a graphene patch structure, showing that the line waves produced can operate in the optical range.
The design involves a graphene surface integrated with an epsilon near zero substrate, which considers the effects of both dual and uniform reactive impedances.
However, this work specifically focuses on utilizing line waves in dual impedance structures.

One of the most effective approaches to building intelligent robotic systems is Learning from Demonstration (LfD), however research is still needed to overcome challenges such as multi-agent learning and prolonged autonomy.  A new architecture for multi-agent LfD is introduced which enables the creation of reliable and efficient robotic systems in complex and large-scale environments by leveraging advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) through the implementation of a Federated Learning (FL)-based collaborative learning environment involving both humans and robots. This novel approach capitalizes on local edge computing and AI-driven processes at multiple robotic platforms to generate a unified, AI-driven global model that accommodates variations across distributed environments. This innovative framework extends the traditional LfD method by integrating: (1) a unified model aggregation mechanism that accommodates local discrepancies, (2) the ability to learn and adapt without constant human supervision, (3) a mechanism to seamlessly add new robotic learners, and (4) the ability to remove existing learners without affecting the system's performance. Evaluations within a simulated environment confirmed the architecture's capability to operate effectively across distributed settings with multiple robotic agents, demonstrating its potential to overcome LfD's limitations and paving the way for more advanced cognitive AI architectures.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction.  To overcome this limitation, a modified objective function is introduced, allowing for regular bias correction through regularity and asymptotic properties.  Establishing the model's consistency, along with the regularity assumptions required, is also a key focus of this research.  Similar contributions have been made in the fields of least squares and bi-linear regression.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting subject-object relationships in a graph. Currently, the
main challenge in achieving great results lies in the substantial data disparities
between these two objectives. Our study puts forth a novel strategy to overcome
this issue by applying knowledge graph link prediction to enhance relation extraction
models, ultimately resulting in improved accuracy in the final models. Our
