Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy and reveling hidden states.
The examination also uncovered an exchange of electrons based on tunneling, a process that can introduce entanglement and diversify the behavior of electrons within the crystal.
These discoveries lead to the notion that silicon may be used as a material for generating complex, entangled states that could be applied in quantum computing and other fields.

Several disciplines have been influenced by optimization techniques in various real-world scenarios, hence their importance is being increasingly acknowledged by the community. As a result of this growing interest, researchers have been able to develop multiple open-source frameworks for optimization, ultimately contributing to innovation in both techniques and their practical applications. In the context of this study, we introduce a novel framework, known as LibOPT, for efficiently creating and testing optimization algorithms, with a focus on its core features and functionality. By showcasing its versatility, our research demonstrates the use of LibOPT in implementing high-performance proxy-based optimization algorithms, outperforming existing benchmark software in terms of speed and efficiency.

Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine varieties, semi- affine varieties, projective spaces, and rational varieties, while also exploring other related properties.

In non-commutative space-time deformations, the definition of identical particles breaks down. These models are described by non-abelian space symmetries represented by a four-momentum group. Our approach recognizes that for multi-particle states, the total system momentum is the only well-defined property. Calculating the total momentum involves non-commutative composition of individual particle momenta, which become ambiguous. Our results indicate that previous Fock space constructions were flawed due to incorrect assumptions and lack success. We demonstrate that momentum exchange underlies a relativistic covariance principle in the braiding of quantum numbers, solving a persistent challenge in the field.

We apply the two-photon absorption transient current technique to study
properties of CVD-grown single-crystal diamond. This innovative approach uses
a femtosecond laser to investigate transport in 3D, without necessitating
physical sectioning or destruction of the sample. By incorporating a unique
modulation of the electric field, we developed an analytical model that
reverses simulates the carrier distribution, yielding quantitative estimates
of mobile charge density, spatial dimensions, and resistance. This technique
enabled us to distinguish the semiconductor properties of the diamond, by
comparing the measured values of the diamond itself to those of a 100%
hydrogen-terminated sample. The results reveal that the diamond contains
significant levels of hydrogen-related defects which strongly affect its
semiconductor behavior.

Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. These difficulties have caught the attention of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, driving innovative research in the field. In this study, we delve into the advanced techniques for detecting and categorizing misogynistic content on social media platforms, specifically in the Arabic language. We have developed and released the AMT-MG dataset on ground truthed posts that promote misogyny for the purposes of this research. The dataset comprises 14272 posts gathered from Twitter, which we use to train models in this study. The primary challenge posed by the data is the significant imbalance between comments that promote misogyny and their opposing counterparts. We have proposed and evaluated two deep learning models, a multi-task framework that integrates classification and sequence labelling, as well as a separate classifier model. The former uses the same data to guide both tasks, while the latter relies on data separately labelled for both tasks. We have compared our models to various baseline models, which we found out perform better than earlier studies.

This study centres around the solvability of a distinct class of fractional backward stochastic differential equations that take into account past influences within their generators, under Lipschitz condition it's demonstrated that the existence and uniqueness of such equations are assured. Furthermore, a key comparison theorem has been formulated.

We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from PILCO, a method for probabilistic policy search, our research demonstrates that constraining the uncertainty in the Gaussian Process model's distribution, quantified by the KL-divergence, is crucial for developing robust controllers. In contrast to previous approaches, which focused on optimizing the average reward in the mean environment, our novel optimization criterion optimizes the average reward over the probability distribution of scenarios. Theoretical justifications and practical evaluations on simulated robots and real inflatable robots are also included to support our findings.

Several key network communication challenges such as caching and computation are interconnected. A centralized caching system seeks to mitigate network strain during peak wireless network times, whereas distributed computation seeks to expedite the processing of data objects. This paper, drawing inspiration from a study of arithmetic sequences, presents a comprehensive model for creating caching schemes. This model subsumes various existing caching schemes as specialized cases, and we demonstrate that a specific placement strategy, when combined with a broadcast schedule, can achieve optimal caching performance in accordance with a predetermined bound. Furthermore, we find that a specific placement strategy, combined with a specific computation delivery approach, achieves the maximum possible throughput in a distributed computation setting.

We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative framework. To capture the essence of non-terminating processes in PCF, we employ the lifting monad from topos theory, which has been adapted for univalent type theory by Escard\'o and Knapp. Our work confirms that using the lifting monad provides a viable way to handle partiality within univalent type theory, and we also demonstrate that a predicative and constructive Scott model is achievable.

Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$.

Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, demonstrating improved efficiency over prior methods.
Simulation results and real-world testing on a mobile robotic arm are presented, showcasing its ability to navigate through intricate environments while avoiding collisions and achieving faster speeds compared to previous methods.

Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators – sentence overlap and edit distance – are employed for gauging sentence similarity.

Researchers have suggested the application of quantum interferometry and information processing in Bose-Einstein condensates. Although some tasks can be performed with linear transformations, certain complex operations require nonlinear interactions. This study investigates the feasibility of implementing nonlinear quantum gates using a mixture of coherent states and antiphased states. By exploring various evolutionary paths, we have discovered that even a simple beam splitter can execute a crucial nonlinear operation, thereby making multiple controlled beam splittings possible, which is crucial in interferometry and has been demonstrated with successful measurement of entanglement. Additionally, we have shown that multiple beam splittings can be performed sequentially without destroying the quantum nature of the system, which opens up new possibilities for quantum information processing with low-dimensional systems.

This paper aims to accomplish two distinct objectives. Firstly, it seeks to establish a unicity theorem for meromorphic mappings from a complete Kähler manifold to a complex projective space, under the constraint of limited intersection with hypersurfaces. Secondly, the paper aims to prove a unicity theorem for the case of nondegenerate meromorphic mappings that share a specified number of hyperplanes in a particular geometric configuration.

Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. Historically, the nondegenerate locus has been obtained using ideal-theoretic techniques like saturation ideals and equidimensional decompositions. We propose an algorithm leveraging signature-based features of Gröbner basis algorithms to directly calculate the Gröbner basis for the nondegenerate locus closure without initially solving the entire polynomial system through Gröbner basis computation.

Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess in the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass distribution over hadronic contributions, we found that approximately 15-20\% of inclusive $e^{+}e^{-}$ production in Cu$+$Cu collisions at midrapidity and 0-60\% centrality corresponds to non-isolated, low-momentum direct photons. Moreover, we found that the production rate of low-momentum direct photons in Cu$+$Cu collisions is 1.1$\pm$0.6 per collision, which is comparable to Au$+$Au collisions at the same energy.

The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We develop a new method for determining hypergraph extremality and apply it to calculate the asymptotic extremal function of the tetrahedron graph under our novel framework. The codegree squared sum, or co2(G), is introduced to measure codegree magnitude in a 3-uniform hypergraph, with exco2(n,H) representing the maximal codegree squared sum among n-vertex H-free hypergraphs. Utilizing flag algebra computations, we determine the codegree squared extremal numbers for K4^3 and K5^3 and demonstrate associated stability properties, revealing the structural resemblance of extremal K4^3-free hypergraphs to the conjectured extremal hypergraphs of Turan's tetrahedron problem. Additionally, we identify key general characteristics of exco2(n,H), such as the existence of a scaled limit and invariance under vertex blow-up.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy.

Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas, as well as their escape from pulsar wind nebulae. Research on pulsar halos has brought to light that their associated diffusion coefficient is substantially lower than the overall average in the Galaxy, thus generating considerable interest among scientists. We delve into the recent breakthroughs in the study of pulsar halos, including the distinct properties of these sources, identified pulsar halos, theoretical mechanisms underlying their exceptionally slow diffusion, their potential roles in explaining the galactic center excess and a portion of the 75 MHz radio diffuse background, and the implications of these findings for investigating cosmic-ray propagation and particle injection in the Galaxy. Lastly, we outline the prospective research avenues for future research.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather classification system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, developing such a system poses challenges due to weather-related data scarcity and unpredictable variability in weather conditions.
In response to these challenges, our research introduces the RFS dataset, captures relevant images from the RFS dataset, and conducts a comprehensive evaluation of the state-of-the-art convolutional neural network approaches for weather classification.

Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later.

Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In response, researchers have turned to data-driven methods. However, current methods typically require extensive model learning through numerous simulations or offline processes, which often fail to adapt to novel scenarios or objects encountered during online operation. In this research, we propose an innovative online algorithm that uses the Koopman operator theory to update and refine a dynamic model in real-time, integrating visual feedback via an onboard camera. By integrating a model predictive control strategy, the algorithm can adjust the gripper's movement to achieve the desired object grasping. We evaluated our approach by attempting to pick and grasp objects in a diverse set of 16 tasks, successfully updating the model within 10-30 seconds and successfully completing the tasks at a high rate of 80-100%.

One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the lowest cost value for a given function, known as an optimization problem. Various numerical methods have been proposed to solve this problem, but the Gradient Descent method remains the most popular due to its ease and effectiveness. Nonetheless, this approach faces challenges with local minima and slow convergence, particularly when near the optimal point. In response, researchers developed the Natural Gradient Descent method to improve performance across multiple domains, including machine learning, tensor networks, and quantum algorithms. Our work presents a new method to further expand upon NGD, utilizing a suitable reference manifold to expedite convergence and enhance understanding of optimization methods.

High-energy emissions from ancient supermassive black holes can provide a direct look through cosmic dust and gas, while those from more typical black holes are often obscured by dust emission. A nearby massive black hole with a mass equivalent to over a billion times that of our sun has been found at a great distance and is surrounded by a massive, ancient structure. Researchers have discovered a massive black hole at the center of a distant galaxy and are studying its surrounding environment to better understand the area. Researchers have found that a massive black hole at the center of a distant galaxy is surrounded by a massive, ancient structure and are studying its environment to better understand the area.

This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients,
and we introduce the LSPrognostic net, a novel probabilistic model that leverages
text, image, and patient data to forecast survival times. The model's probabilistic
forecasting nature allows for prediction uncertainty to be considered. The
robustness of our model was tested through data augmentation and sensitivity
analyses. The findings reveal that incorporating both textual and visual information
significantly enhances survival time predictions, resulting in a 30% increase in mean
absolute error reduction compared to models using individual modalities in isolation.
Moreover, the model's uncertainty estimates align with clinical observations, and
we found that patients' life expectancy can be prolonged by up to six months through
personalized treatment suggestions.

A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques and measures used to create and model natural language states, uncovering both successful applications and unresolved challenges in the field.

A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra analysis. By leveraging sophisticated simulations of cosmic structure formation, a substantial synthetic dataset of absorption spectra and associated 1D matter densities is generated. With this dataset, a series of machine learning models are constructed to predict matter density power spectra. We achieve reconstruction accuracy of approximately 1% for certain wavelengths while noting a corresponding error increase at higher wavelengths. Furthermore, we investigate the size of datasets required to attain a specified error rate, highlighting the data requirements for a desired level of accuracy. This work lays the groundwork for analyzing the forthcoming large-scale datasets anticipated with future observational facilities.

This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type. Firstly, we establish the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to U(∅) are weight modules. We then find the conditions under which the restrictions of non-weight modules over the Lie algebra A(k) are weight modules. Finally, we identify the requirements for the Lie algebra representation to be free over U(∅) when considering the Lie algebra A(k) special case.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial manual labor to define conversation topics,
handle user inquiries, and ensure the system can integrate with existing platforms.
This paper introduces a novel approach using role-specification to enable the
efficient construction of scalable chat systems capable of meeting various
performance and deployment needs. Role-specification enables the formulation
of logical predicates describing desired user and system responses within the
conversation. This approach enables the direct incorporation of natural language
specifications to train open-domain dialogue models, thereby eliminating the
need for extensive and costly topic definition, inquiry handling, and system
integration. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by applying role-
specification to two real-world use cases. Furthermore, our method can be found
at https://github.com/lyboyo/Open-Domain-Dialogue/Role_Specification.

The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbance known as the stochastic gravitational wave memory background (SGWMB). Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is proportional to the inverse square of frequency. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics allow it to span a broader frequency range due to its non-smooth, discontinuous nature. The occurrence rate of massive, intermediate-metallicity supernovae driven by magnetic forces produces an initial peak in SGWMB at a frequency of about 1 Hz. The presence of SGWMB can be detected using the same methods employed to find its steady-state counterpart, and its amplitude will be within the detection limits of future gravitational wave observatories such as LISA. The Gravitational Wave memory detector concept may be effective in finding SGWMB, and the device's sensitivity will be sufficient for LISA, but several configurations will be required to gather an SGWMB dataset.

A hypothetical supersymmetry framework offers an explanation for why large particles weren't discovered by the Large Hadron Collider; this framework predicts the universe underwent a phase transition around the time of the universe's birth that may create ripples in space time that scientists could detect. Developing a realistic model based on how this supersymmetry is broken, researchers found this phase transition can lead to masses in certain heavy particles that may create more particles and a new theory of matter, as well as distortions in space time that may contain information about the universe's early days. The universe's early moments can be explained by a chain of events starting with a period when particles are out of balance, leading to a large number of particles, some of which become balanced and lead to matter particles. The balance shift, or symmetry breaking, can be explained by a change in the universe's state, such as when particles move from a more ordered to a less ordered state, like a solid becoming liquid. The balance shift can create ripples in space time that may contain information about the universe's early days. The model predicts a change in the universe's state can lead to masses in certain heavy particles, a phenomenon called mass generation. A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity to diverse users and services. A novel approach to this challenge is presented, incorporating an emergent signaling game framework with a neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence system that facilitates causal reasoning. To design a context-specific communication language, an alternating maximization algorithm optimizes utility values between communication nodes. This language enhances the vocabulary for message transmission by splitting complex data into simpler components and allowing for multi-step causal reasoning. A neural network model is used to implement the language, and an analysis of its efficiency is conducted, demonstrating improved performance with the new language. Simulation outcomes confirm the results and showcase the key features of this semantic communication design.

The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the last few decades. A primary factor driving this attention was the development of large linguistic databases and wordnet - a foundational concept in linguistic research since the 1990s. These databases and related ideas have significantly influenced NLP research, facilitating both automatic and semi-manual word meaning associations. This study proposes an innovative approach to word prediction, combining Naive Bayes and Latent Knowledge concepts to maximize associativity in linguistic databases.

Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with high recall rates compared to conventional techniques. Recent examples include STAMP and NARM models, which, however, did not perform as expected on Zalando's Fashion-Similar dataset in comparison to a basic collaborative-filtering method. Our proposed strategy targets improving item ranking by leveraging the encoded session information through an attention network and demonstrates the potential through Candidate Rank Embedding in re-ranking. Experimental results demonstrate a considerable enhancement over the baseline on metrics such as Recall, MRR, and Click-Through-Rate in an online setting, and we further observed improvements when applied to STAMP and NARM models on two public real-world datasets for the task of next-click prediction.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a phase diagram. This diagram classifies dimer configurations based on their tactic behavior and also indicates how some dimers can maintain direction and achieve greater persistence in motion. This study provides valuable insights into the design of autonomous, responsive colloidal systems that can navigate according to varying activity levels in their environment.

A thorough approach is outlined to simulate single-phase flow in fractured porous media. The proposed methodology comprises three core components: generating an accurate 3D mesh of a fracture network, solving governing equations using a high-order numerical method, and implementing high-performance computing strategies. A mesh generation technique that handles problematic cases to maintain high mesh quality is provided. A versatile simulator utilizes process kernels to enable flexible interactions between the fracture and matrix domains. The efficacy of the methodology is demonstrated through several challenging examples, including instances with numerous fractures, complex fracture connections, and disparate fracture and matrix fluid flow properties.

This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Two key issues arise in achieving these goals: firstly, determining optimal strategies to temporarily disband the formation to avoid collisions (collision avoidance reformation), and secondly, effecting this reformation while minimizing the time and energy spent by the drones. To resolve the first challenge, a cellular automata-based method is utilized to identify efficient formations that evade obstacles while reducing time and energy consumption. To tackle the second issue, a near-optimal reformation strategy after successful collision avoidance is realized through a temperature function reduction technique borrowed from the point set registration process. The objective of this reformation process is to rapidly decrease the distance between the swarm's original and temporary formations. To quantify the success of these techniques, a metric called formation distance squared (FDQS) is employed along with a measure of convergence rate to evaluate the efficiency of the registration process. Experimental outcomes confirm that the approach offers swift convergence and substantial FDQS reductions.

This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the minimum number of unique eigenvalues, eigenvalue limits, the characteristic polynomial, and bounds for the Seidel energy of a chain graph, which outperform previously proposed energy bounds by Haemers. We also obtain the minimum Seidel energy for specific chain graphs of order $n$, along with presenting several unresolved questions.

In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which defies the criteria for being a Markov process or semi-martingale, we resort to the fractional White noise calculus and specialized tools for differentiating functions of measures to establish necessary and sufficient stochastic maximum principles. This approach is further exemplified by two applications, including solving a delayed consumption optimization problem from a cash flow and a linear-quadratic problem under delay constraints.

We've developed a unique, detailed two-parameter set of finite-band Jacobi elliptic potentials that correspond to the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator, seamlessly linking two well-known limit cases, each associated with the absence or presence of elliptic parameters. To thoroughly analyze the Dirac operator's spectrum, we've made connections between periodic/antiperiodic eigenvalue problems for the operator, equivalent tridiagonal operator actions in weighted Hilbert spaces and relevant Heun equation connection issues. This, in turn, ties into four related non-self-adjoint, unbounded tridiagonal operator eigenvalue problems which surprisingly possess real eigenvalues.

RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with users; however, congestion areas are often poorly served due to high data traffic, weak signals, and interference, which can be addressed through the use of vehicle relays. To enhance the network in these situations, this research utilizes stochastic geometry to develop an innovative analytical framework for the performance of these networks in congested areas. Our findings reveal that the addition of vehicle relays significantly improves the coverage of vehicles in congested areas, leading to better data transfer rates and reduced network latency. This, in turn, enables a range of safety-critical applications, such as vehicle-based relaying of emergency messages, and providing communication services to vehicles in areas with weak RSU coverage.

Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To resolve this, we developed an automated system that examines semantic modifications in Wikipedia edits to create labels, considering the pre-edit version as an example requiring improvement, and high-quality sentences as instances that need no improvement. By employing our labels in machine learning models, we found that performance improves over relying on existing, manually generated labels. Furthermore, we discovered that Wikipedia editors' behavior provides more accurate labels compared to crowdworkers who lack the same level of contextual understanding and agreement as editors.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's quality is measured by the similarity between the model's output and the network it's based on, in terms of distributional metrics like KL-divergence. This is used to formulate a new objective function which combines the model's ability to accurately produce decisions with its ability to accurately represent the original network's distribution. This study also presents methods for actively selecting training samples that effectively integrate knowledge from both the network and the distillation model, and shows that a model trained using these samples can achieve higher accuracy and improve decision-making performance even if the original data is unavailable. Additionally, the study conducts a comprehensive analysis of the presented approach on multiple image classification datasets, and provides a publicly available implementation of the proposed method.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^4$-actions, we establish a simple method for achieving this transformation. Our work rigorously addresses almost abelian solvmanifolds across arbitrary dimensions, providing clear group-theoretic criteria for determining actions that are free, proper, and isometric.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this problem. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agent can learn from its companion's accomplishments without expert input, improving performance more efficiently than existing methods.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing the probability of incorrect paths as the computing depth increases. We also prove that the proposed metric function maintains a lower bound on the polarized cutoff rate and provide a mathematical expression for this bound. We evaluate the distance between codewords using the symmetric weight spectrum and analyze the expected distance between codewords. We also introduce a measure for quantifying the distance between codewords, which is closely related to the proposed metric function, while providing upper and lower bounds for this measure. We use the Q-function and entropy functions to calculate the expected distance between codewords and obtain approximate numerical results that confirm the exponential reduction of the expected distance as the computing depth increases. We compare the error-correction performance of our approach with that of deep neural network-based approaches, observing improved performance for low-rate PAC codes.

This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud-based hand joint tracking system, to calculate hand joint movement between frames. Our novel hand pose canonicalization module simplifies this task and enables accurate tracking of hand joints. By converting these joints into a template-based hand model called MANO, our system can reconstruct the entire hand. To track objects, we use an efficient module to generate object SDF data and perform optimization-based reconstruction. Our method is the first sequence-to-sequence 3D hand pose estimation system, allowing for tracking hands in sequential frames. We evaluate its performance on two public datasets and find that our method performs close to or better than current state-of-the-art hand tracking methods when tracking multiple hands over time. To validate its effectiveness in real-world scenarios, we collected and made available a new public dataset called HOHI-5F. Our code and dataset are open for access.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 5, 4, 3, or 2 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field and demonstrates that the reduced group retains its properties regardless of the used prime in the reduction process.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning and relies on only one training process, enabling effortless conversion of any calibration setup into a reliable real-world calibration system. Furthermore, our system's dependence on real-time object recognition being accurate is minimal, as it includes a pose estimation module that employs a universal end-effector database and deep learning-based object detection for efficient integration with the calibration process.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a star are being conducted. In the core of a star that has not yet undergone nuclear reactions, it's found that the interactions between these particles and the star's constituent atoms via a particular particle can produce an unusually high number of neutrinos, which could equal and potentially exceed the star's initial nuclear reaction neutrino emissions. This process primarily involves two reactions: a collision of two dark matter particles resulting in neutrinos or intermediate particles that then decay into neutrinos, which further involves the transformation of these particles into pseudoscalar mediators within the star's dense environment. This investigation demonstrates that in a star with certain composition and a specific mass of dark matter particles per unit volume, the total number of neutrinos produced per unit volume and per unit time can range from a fraction of percent to over ninety percent of the star's initial nuclear reaction neutrino emissions. This process is anticipated to be most pronounced in stars with lower mass and higher concentrations of dark matter particles. This investigation confirms that in a star with properties similar to the Sun, the concentration of dark matter particles within it is below $10^{16}$ g/cm$^3$ and the mass of dark matter particles is below a few hundred GeV.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has partnered with CFIS for $r$-band data collection, boasting exceptional seeing of 0.65 arcseconds and complete magnitude 24.5 for precise weak-lensing research. Our analysis covers an expansive 1700 square degrees of the sky, cataloging 40 million galaxies, translating to a density of 6.8 per square arcminute. A low-level systematic bias was found in this research, providing a groundwork for extensive cosmological studies when the full 4800 square degree survey is completed. Introducing ShapePipe, a cutting-edge pipeline leveraging Ngmix for precise galaxy shape detection and metacalibration for accurate shear calibration, the study extensively validates the pipeline through Point Spread Function, galaxy shape tests, and realistic simulations to minimize systematics. The analysis encompasses two datasets, '3P' and '4P', distinguishing between them in terms of depth and residual systematic bias. The shear two-point correlation function was measured for both datasets, revealing a signal that aligns with the predicted cosmological values, albeit with margins of error that include zero.

A notable consequence of a finding made by Veech more than 50 years ago, relating to the mod $2$ form of the Kronecker-Weyl theorem, has to do with sequences of irrational rotations of the form $\{q\alpha\}$. In the event that a certain number $\alpha$ resists being closely approximated by rational numbers and another number $b$ in the interval $(0,1)$ differs from the rotation sequence for no integer $m$, then, as $N$ approaches infinity, the parity of the sizes of sets consisting of numbers of the form $\{q\alpha\}$ within the interval $[0,b)$ that correspond to $q$ values up to $N$ displays evenly distributed occurrences.

The text also discusses how it answers a query put forth by Veech, thereby providing a revised mod $n$ form of a prior result (as stated in Theorem 3.1). A characterization, based on specific values, of scenarios where evenly distributed occurrences result (especially when $b$ equals the rotation sequence for some natural number $m$ and $\alpha$ is an irrational number) is also proposed (as stated in Theorem 2.1). We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

Researchers found that a specific type of magnetic material, applied to a thin
film of the material called yttrium iron garnet, can cause the material to reach
a state known as Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) correlations. BKT correlations
are a key characteristic of materials that are on the verge of becoming
magnetically disordered. What's unique about this finding is that BKT correlations
usually only occur in materials that can easily be disturbed by their surroundings,
known as spin glasses, or in extremely thin layers of materials that are applied
with a uniform external magnetic field. In this study, the BKT correlations were
observed to be highly responsive to an external magnetic field, making it a
very versatile tool to study this effect. By using a specialized technique to
measure the material's magnetic response, the researchers were able to confirm
that the observed changes in the material's behavior were indeed caused by BKT
correlations. The researchers also used this technique to determine the temperature
at which BKT correlations began to form in the material, known as the BKT transition
temperature, and found that it could be adjusted by changing the external magnetic
field. The observed changes in the material's behavior were found to be consistent
with the predictions of the BKT theory, known as $2-\eta$ scaling. This study provides
further evidence that the BKT correlations are not simply a fictional state,

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In this study, we explore the interplay between the axion-like particles and right-handed neutrinos, particularly focusing on how their relationships impact dark matter distributions within the axion-like particles' potential landscapes.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, surpassing the previous best-known estimate of $\alpha\leq 0.463$. This advancement allows for the development of a classical algorithm capable of approximating the output probabilities of $n$-qubit Clifford + T circuits $U$ within a specified inverse polynomial error margin, using a time complexity of $\mathrm{poly}(n,m)2^{\alpha m}$. Furthermore, the investigation yields refined bounds on the stabilizer rank of symmetric product states $|\psi\rangle^{\otimes m}$, ultimately leading to the creation of a strong simulation algorithm for circuits comprising Clifford gates and multiple instances of a fixed single-qubit Z-rotation gate, operating at a time complexity of $\text{poly}(n,m) 2^{m/2}$. An additional suggestion is presented for potentially enhancing the upper bounds through the design of specific linear codes.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters for the energy 
density equation of state within the FRW universe, analogous to a quintessence model.
We will reassess complex quintessence by modifying its potential and analyzing 
scalar field dynamics, followed by evaluating the differences in and stability 
of two scenarios, namely non-interacting and interacting.
We will examine the plausibility of these scenarios by calculating the fractional 
energy density, $\Omega_{D}$, and analyzing two distinct cases for the fractional
equation of state, $\omega_{Q}$, to determine the quintessence-like complex field 
redshift, $\psi$.
Furthermore, we will visualize the instability regions of two scenarios in a 
$\omega_{Q}$-$Q$-matter table, and discuss our findings.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study involved conducting multiple spectroscopic observations on specific areas of the Galactic plane. After data collection, the team applied the LAMOST Spectral Fitting Tool to process and analyze the optical spectra of ground-based telescopes, achieving a high level of spectral accuracy. By determining radial velocities, the team created H-R diagrams for each region and derived other essential astrophysical properties. As a result, the study identified 93,804 distinct sources with radial velocity, of which 50.1% are new discoveries. Furthermore, the study provided essential data for navigating a challenging region of interest for the Galactic plane, a area that presents absorption and scattering challenges due to its proximity to the Galactic plane.

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, termed TuRaN, which utilizes a lower supply voltage than recommended to cause SRAM access failures, then applies the SHA-256 hash function to these faults to create high-throughput random numbers. We validate the practicality of TuRaN through SPICE simulations on diverse process nodes and assess its reliability through real-world experiments conducted on two commercial FPGA boards. Furthermore, we demonstrate the high quality of the random numbers produced by TuRaN using the NIST standard randomness tests and note its exceptional performance with respect to throughput, energy consumption, and latency.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules that interact electrostatically: one molecule is a single-electron transistor and the other is a single-electron trap. To confirm our design's validity, a theoretical analysis was performed, integrating ab-initio electronic structure calculations with a general single-electron tunneling theory. The outcomes demonstrate that these tiny molecular constructs can process electrical signals at extremely high speeds while also storing information over extended periods and exhibiting a substantial ratio between active and inactive current levels. Additionally, simulations have shown that self-organized monolayers built from these molecules could also function as resistive switches with comparable properties and the capacity to withstand flaws and irregularities in electrical charges.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. In this discussion, we explore the application of all-loop causal representation to describe multi-loop Feynman integrands, which can be characterized by loop topological features and connections. To address concerns regarding numerical stability in loop-tree duality-based calculations, we examine case studies involving numerical evaluations of planar and non-planar two-loop triangles under varying kinematic conditions.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof that shows the similarity between the time-evolution operator for a one-dimensional quantum walk with two possible states and the hydrogen atom, allowing us to apply a method similar to eigenfunction expansion to find the probability amplitude as a sum of the walk's eigenstates.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to around three times the mass of our sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical behavior within a linearly coupled $q$-deformed optomechanical system. Analyzing the developed system, which consists of two deformed cavities interacting with mechanical mirrors and coupled through an external field, yields unexpected amplification of optical phenomena. The observed amplification arises from interactions influencing both mechanical and optical components. The analysis reveals that hybridized modes near the system's eigenfrequencies can produce amplification by aligning with specific $q$-deformation values. Notably, this system can create amplification even when far from these eigenfrequencies. Depending on the mechanical mass, orientation, and driving power on the optical field, the system can produce transparency or amplification. The observed amplification can reach a considerable level, as indicated by large $\mathcal{T}$ and $A$ values. Furthermore, the system can produce amplification due to light, which is confirmed through analysis of various optical characteristics. Consequently, $q$-deformed optomechanical systems offer valuable research platforms for exploring and understanding new optical phenomena.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections in a plane that aligns with the rotors' symmetry axes, resulting in R-negative states with positive parity. Furthermore, I established a connection between reflections and R-operations, relating them to specific internal changes within the rotors, which I then used to calculate and compare the electromagnetic transition strengths of these states with those of their positive scissors mode counterparts.

The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate a monolayer of strontium vanadate grown on a substrate to investigate the thickness-induced metal-to-insulator transition. We found that two different terminations lead to the same insulating behavior at equilibrium but exhibit distinct behavior when doped or subjected to a gate voltage. Through many-body calculations, we revealed various nonlocal fluctuations resulting from antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, stripe, and checkerboard orbital ordering instabilities. By considering the role of orbital degrees of freedom, we explain how these instabilities emerge and demonstrate how ultra-thin film reconstruction and changes to coordination polyhedra result in unique material properties.

The occurrence of diffusion can be seen across various natural phenomena, and this widespread application is attributed to the broad implications of the central limit theorem. In the past, scientists discovered an extension of typical dynamics, resulting in "anomalous" diffusion that accounts for distributions characterized by long, power-law tails. One such physical system - laser-cooled atomic ensembles - offers a controlled environment to study such phenomena. In this study, researchers derived analytical equations governing the persistence length and autocorrelation function of cold-atomic ensembles within dissipative optical lattices. These equations demonstrate how anomalous statistics influence diffusion and reveal a distinct classification of universality classes based on specific laser-cooling techniques. To validate their theoretical findings, researchers used numerical simulations, thereby providing a comprehensive theoretical framework that can be experimentally verified to refine our understanding of anomalous statistics in laser-cooled atomic systems.

This study investigates the effects of information dissemination on cryptocurrency trading volumes by examining both pairwise and high-order interactions within the cryptocurrency trading network. By implementing a Granger causality analysis and testifying the significance of real returns, we validate our approach. The results reveal that higher-order connections predominate in cryptocurrency trading, and analysis of trading volume suggests that they facilitate the dissemination of information, whereas returns are primarily influenced by pairwise connections. Moreover, we observe long-distance influences in both pairwise and high-order networks, implying that they arise from either investor attention or price volatility.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei that facilitate the creation of clouds due to their role in overcoming extremely high supersaturated conditions needed for homogeneous water droplet formation. Research has revealed that the complex intermolecular motions of growing clusters play a vital part in this process. However, the significance of quantum effects, specifically zero-point motion, in this process remains unclear. Our study investigates this question using a novel variational determination of vibrational states within a potential energy surface, applying the approach to small clusters of sulphuric acid and water. Our results show that accounting for quantum effects does not significantly influence the growth rates of these clusters, and the underlying chemistry remains largely unchanged. Nonetheless, the incorporation of quantum effects reveals novel and highly energetic states that could implicate a new acid-base interaction between components and hold potential for future research.

We introduce a novel notion of compactification for sets comprised of perception pairs, which adheres to specific requirements. This development is pivotal in mapping the space of group equivariant non-expansive operators to a topological space that satisfies rigorous standards.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity in fluids. In studying this, researchers investigate whether this analogy holds for materials that conduct energy and charge. They examine the response to various gradients - including gravity, electric potential, and temperature - in a special class of 2D materials known as $\mathrm{InSe}$. By combining precise measurements of electrical resistance and heat flow, assisted by unique edge states that allow for sensitive detection of changes, the researchers demonstrate that this analogy breaks and traditional relationships fail. Notably, this occurs because the materials' responses to gravity and temperature gradients differ significantly. This finding opens up new avenues for exploring unusual phenomena in materials that conduct energy and charge.

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By combining theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we demonstrate that several widespread training heuristics, such as parameter and spectral regularization, as well as parameter initialization techniques, serve to control geometric complexity.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), among others, in solving automated essay grading.  Our study focuses on the effectiveness of transformer-based architectures, specifically BERT and RoBERTa, in conjunction with data augmentation methods for developing a versatile and efficient automated essay grading model across diverse topics.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from such marginal independence models, with a specific focus on models for random graphs and matroids' independent set polytopes. We also explore numerical methods for parameter estimation through both Euclidean distance and maximum likelihood techniques. Our analysis shows that simultaneous estimation for all parameters can be achieved with precision, whereas individual estimation may not provide exact results. We also establish a criterion for identifiability and investigate the asymptotic normality of estimators.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to higher socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate relationships between different socioeconomical groups in various societal settings.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS consensus mechanisms provides a reasonable trade-off for enabling a more efficient and scalable decentralised cryptocurrency with preserved anonymity capabilities.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons simultaneously produced in high-energy collisions between protons.  These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's data set that contains 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of information.  Separate searches for individual combinations of bosons, including W boson variations, have been done using several patterns of final particle arrangements.  Together, the signals for these processes indicate a cross-section of boson creation that is slightly larger than that predicted by the standard model, occurring 5.7 (expected to be 5.9) standard deviations above background noise.  Specifically, signals for individual W boson variations have a significance of around 3.3 to 3.4 standard deviations and the measured rates of boson creation are also recorded.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. This research paper readdresses this issue by presenting a new, open-access UD Hebrew treebank. This corpus, created by sampling various topics from Hebrew Wikipedia, provides a much-needed upgrade to NLP's understanding of contemporary Hebrew. The project evaluates its own annotations, validates results using automated tools, and achieves new state-of-the-art results on UD NLP tasks by combining advanced language models with innovative approaches. Additionally, the project updates and releases the existing UD HTB annotation scheme, incorporating the improvements from the new Hebrew corpus.

We present a strictly $\varepsilon$-isometric embedding of any incompressible $m$-dimensional subset of $\ell_p$ into $\mathbb{R}^N$, where the dimensionality reduction map, the lifting map, and the precision parameter $\varepsilon$ depend on $m$, $p$, and $\varearepsilon$. The embedding constant is influenced by $m$, $p$, and $\varepsilon$, remaining bounded as $m$ grows. The results extend the findings of Alaei and Pajor ($m=1$), Alaei and El Becherifi ($m=1$ again), and Krahel and Osekowski ($p\in [1,\infty)$. $m\leq \frac{1}{\ln2}$). Furthermore, for $p\in (1,\infty)$, we explore properties of random matrices whose entries are independent, identically distributed, and symmetric. These matrices serve as dimensionality reduction maps with a row norm greater than $\sqrt{\ln2}$ and establish a lower bound on the smallest possible absolute row norm of any dimensionality reduction map.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research institutions with extensive resources and diverse expertise, we believe universities can play a pivotal role in cooperative modeling. By collaborating, institutions can pool their data and knowledge to create more comprehensive and accurate models, benefiting each other and producing valuable research outcomes.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions and neglect the effects of degree correlations. However, in practical scenarios, LDPC codes with varying degree structures are constructed using iterative methods such as cyclic coding, which lead to degree correlations. This research aims to understand the performance of LDPC codes that exhibit degree correlations, specifically those resulting from cyclic encoding. We calculate the maximum mutual information of the encoder and decoder of these degree-correlated LDPC codes, where the encoder employs a binary erasure probability $p_{\rm er}$-based cyclic interference pattern and the decoder uses a binary erasure decoding approach on a square grid representation of the parity-check matrix. Our analysis shows that degree correlations reduce the maximum mutual information of the encoder and decoder compared to LDPC codes with non-correlated degrees, with this decrease more pronounced for codes with higher cyclic interference patterns and lower $p_{\rm er}$ values. We also observe that degree correlations lower the threshold value $p_{\rm er,th}(M)$ in binary erasure channels, with this impact more significant for LDPC codes with higher cyclic interference patterns and lower $p_{\rm er}$ values. Furthermore, we found that degree correlations increase the minimum required degree $D_{\rm min}$ in the degree distribution and affect the distribution shape, with higher cyclic interference patterns resulting in more pronounced and nonlinear variations in the relative error probability $\mathbb{P}_{

An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded state space safety zone for a control signal, which is ultimately optimized to meet target performance standards. In contrast to the original MPSF, which has difficulties with scalability due to its large number of variables, the new design demonstrates improved computational efficiency without compromising safety guarantees or performance quality. This innovation enables safer adoption of MPSF in large-scale industrial automation where computational demands are high.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's size and domain on the performance of a Korean-centric model. Notably, we discovered that using relevant in-context data for a task results in shot-count-related learning curve patterns, which in turn correlate with model performance. Furthermore, we found that using relevant pretraining data for a task results in better model performance, but also decreases the shape parameter of the learning curve, indicating a wider generalization gap for tasks from unrelated domains. Our research provides empirical evidence for modeling in-context learning using the scViOLE framework and suggests that domain-knowledge prior to pretraining is essential for achieving better model performance in few-shot learning tasks.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of these formations disintegrates. To investigate the long-term effects of this process, we conducted 30 magnetohydrodynamic simulations of kiloparsec-scale, kiloparsec cold clouds within a galaxy cluster environment, considering various initial conditions. Our results indicate that filamentary segments of these clouds quickly cool and separate from the surrounding hot intracluster medium before ultimately fragmenting and creating numerous smaller clumps. These fragments act as nuclei, fostering further condensation through processes such as Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, thereby potentially accounting for the observed parsec-scale filaments and stars within the galaxy cluster neighborhood. It's been discovered that the rate of cloud fragmentation is directly affected by factors like the strength of magnetic fields and thermal conduction, while massive, gravitationally stable clouds may form if magnetic fields are strong and cooling is inefficient, potentially growth of these structures could lead to biases in the observed distribution of cold gas within the galaxy cluster, affecting the measurement of its density and the strength of the magnetic fields and thermal conduction.

The examination of $C\!P$ violation in beauty- and charm-hadron decays serves as
a crucial test of the Standard Model's predictions, also acting as a sensitive
indicator to uncover physical phenomena not accounted for within the SM. The
presentation includes precise measurements of observables connected to the
unitary triangles stemming from unitarity constraints on the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-
Maskawa matrix describing quark mixing, alongside recent $C\!P$ violation
measurements in beauty- and charm-hadrons. Specific emphasis is given to an
analysis that initially reported $C\!P$ violation in beauty baryons and has
since been refined with expanded data.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have unique polarization properties and their high-energy behavior can be described by a newly proposed coefficient model. This model suggests a crucial role for D0-operators in string theory and can be verified by analyzing newly discovered string scattering processes. These processes, representing the most complex string interactions to date, were calculated using a newly developed string scattering approach and their results match those obtained from Gross's earlier formula evaluations. Additionally, the new strings' high-energy interactions can be described by a set of universally applicable mathematical equations, highlighting a key role for differential forms in string theory.

To effectively manage their share of the traffic, cellular service providers are considering policies like cap-exoling "hotspot-ing" where mobile operators limit in-town connectivity to non-subscribing users. This cap-exoling involves core network procedures to block or redirect user traffic, which are usually configured through lookup tables.
