However, these tables must be dynamically updated in line with changing user location, and replacing the existing static configuration method necessitates new management procedures. Furthermore, to respond to surges in demand, mobile operators require the ability to temporarily scale up their networks, which might necessitate the activation of temporary facilities. The management of these facilities, set up to meet exceptional network demands, calls for new management methods to ensure their efficient integration into existing networks. In this article, we explore the potential scenarios for these core network management procedures, and the required changes to existing management systems, in line with the requirements of sustainable and self-organizing 5G cellular networks.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. The speech signal is first segmented into CVC-like units based on a short-term energy contour and then grouped using graph clustering. The clustered units are initialized to include transient onset and decays, and steady-state rhyme components, and are subsequently rearranged into acoustic units in an HMM-GMM framework. The AU sequences are then used to develop synthesis models, and the effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated through the analysis of subjective and objective scores on the Zerospeech 2019 challenge database. The results show that acceptable quality speech synthesis at a low bit rate can be achieved with the proposed method.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of walking and climbing experiments on a 10 kg hexapod robot.

We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource metric.
This approach led to the discovery that the metric is not only necessary, but also sufficient, for one-shot resource conversion in various resource theories, effectively rendering more restrictive protocols unnecessary.
By employing this metric, we were able to refine the performance limits of one-shot and multi-copy probabilistic resource distillation protocols.
Concurrently, we introduced a comprehensive technique for calculating achievable probabilities in resource transformations through a series of convex optimisation problems.
This approach enabled us to precisely assess the trade-offs between probabilities and errors in the distillation of maximally resource-rich states.
Furthermore, we successfully demonstrated the efficacy of our methods in the analysis of quantum entanglement distillation.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The point where excitation occurred had a significant impact on observed dynamics, leading to an infinite number of resonant frequencies in the vertical case and semistability occurring at specific resonant frequencies in the horizontal case. Observations made during experiments align well with model predictions, showing that resonant phenomena can easily be triggered under normal daily conditions of motion.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues to utilize our research to determine non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field strengths and mass accumulation rates. The data show that strongly magnetized clouds produce fast-moving jets only when the protostar gains a relatively small amount of mass per year, typically no more than 10 to the minus 3 solar masses. However, this low-mass rate also results in weakly driven outflows, indicating a paradox. But if high-velocity jets help drive low-velocity outflows, the material ejected in jets should be detectable in clouds with high mass accumulation rates, contradicting observations. To resolve the discrepancy, highly collimated, high-velocity jets must quickly merge with slower outflows, a scenario observable only under high mass accumulation rates, unless highly magnetized. Otherwise, the high-velocity jets remain isolated and dissipate quickly, a scenario observable only at low mass accumulation rates. Data also suggest that for high mass accumulation rates, low-velocity outflows are likely powered by low-velocity jets, a phenomenon that could be detectable with future high-dynamic-range simulations, or if magnetic forces weaken, making highly collimated jets a rarity.

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety strategy with built-in saturation protection, yielding better outcomes than traditional BPC, while also outperforming filtered backstepping and adaptive control methods without incorporating performance and safety features. A comparative analysis between two potential solutions - performance safety with and without prediction - is also presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed strategy.

This research project seeks to offer fresh perspectives on how various gravitational interactions affect an object orbiting the Earth, specifically considering its shape and the impact of sunlight pressure. To achieve this, it provides mathematical predictions and numerical simulations that identify key periods and locations in the object's motion, taking into account its area-to-mass ratio, initial conditions, and the object's variations in distance from the Earth. Such studies are crucial for predicting the behavior of artificial satellites over extended periods.

Semiempirical tight-binding models used to describe electronic structures, often incorporating spin-orbit coupling and using atomic-like wavefunctions, typically involve coordinate systems tied to individual atoms. These models generally aren't constructed with symmetries or transformations in mind. However, in this study, we develop a rigorous approach to ensure that a specific tight-binding model describing transition-metal atoms is insensitive to gauge changes. In this methodology, we carefully define the magnetic vector and evaluate the magnetic field, strictly adhering to gauge invariance principles. We test the methodology's effectiveness by applying it to models of rare-earth and actinide elements.

In a problem focused on category-level perception, we consider utilizing sensor data to identify and understand objects within specific categories despite variations within those categories. An active shape model, where pre-defined CAD models of various objects are used as a reference, is employed to determine the 3D pose and shape of an object. Our first achievement is developing PACE3D* and PACE2D*, which are novel optimisation algorithms ensuring accurate results for both 3D and 2D keypoint data, through the use of precise certifications and robust certification-based search. Additionally, we have improved existing techniques by revising PACE3D and PACE2D, and provided a comprehensive set of experiments for training and testing the models, along with an in-depth analysis of our results. It has been observed that our models are particularly resilient to noisy data and outperform current techniques in various challenging scenarios.

We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it as both a disc and a square using a straightforward formula.

A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups under one protocol. This approach uses Bayesian statistics to optimize sample size and allows information sharing between groups. We develop formulas to ensure each subgroup trial meets specified criteria, comparing the new treatment to a control, by clinically relevant standards. For subgroups with pre-defined similarities, we find the minimum required trial sizes simultaneously. Our approach resembles frequentist methods when there's no sharing of data. Notably, by allowing data borrowing, we find smaller trial sizes needed than traditional methods that don't share information. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach using two actual trials. Further simulations demonstrate our approach maintains accuracy in detecting positive results without increasing false positives.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance between high-speed and high-accuracy. However, conventional control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements, particularly in motion systems that are susceptible to changes based on their position. This research introduces a cutting-edge modification to traditional control designs to address the performance limitations in these systems, effectively allowing for improved motion control even under dynamic conditions. The effectiveness of this innovative approach is showcased through simulation-based testing of a precise moving-magnet planar actuator, known to experience variations based on position during actuation and sensing.

We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment and correspondence issues. Unlike existing methods that require a fully observable shape, PRNet is suited for partial-to-partial registrations, inspired by 2D image matching techniques. This involves self-supervised learning of a suitable geometric representation to capture partial cloud features, and a correspondence estimator that can handle incomplete data. Experimental validation on multiple datasets, including synthetic models and real-world objects, demonstrates PRNet's effectiveness and efficiency compared to other feature-based and learning-based methods.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the quotient $G/\gamma_{c+1}(G)$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. In this research, we derive the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of Generalized Solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$ and explicitly calculate the lower central series for $\Gamma_n$. Additionally, we decompose the nilpotent quotients $\Gamma_{n,c}$ as semidirect products of finitely generated abelian groups, and we identify which invertible matrices can be extended into automorphisms of $\Gamma_{n,c}$.

Instead of presuming hypothetical new physics will be found at future colliders, 
we consider a different possibility where there isn't any. In this case, 
our main goal would be to find out if the unusual Standard Model fits within a vast landscape of possibilities. A crucial step to reach this goal would be to determine the instability scale of the Higgs potential. Achieving this requires pinpointing multiple precise measurements of $m_H$, $I_1$, and $I_2$ or alternatively, $\Gamma_H$ and $c_{12}$. Due to experimental constraints, these measurements may not be obtainable from LHC or FCC-ee. However, a combination of these facilities along with other research options could provide the necessary accuracy.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. What's more, this approach effectively considers the continuity of molecular structures and is resilient against noisy data.

We present the results of the first calculations of the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, specifically $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, $\phi$, $K^*$, and $J/\Psi$. This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for the vector kaon, providing confirmation of lattice QCD predictions; in contrast to expectations, we find a nearly symmetric longitudinal distribution and an obliquely shaped transverse one, indicating a substantial contribution to momentum from the strange quark.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces. Moreover, the paper demonstrates that certain Toeplitz operators are continuous within the context of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, and it provides explicit expressions for the resulting operators.

Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents a significant obstacle in clinical routine tasks due to the additional time and resources required, often making it impractical. Current techniques rely on labels from other modalities or adapt segmentation methods from other domains by tweaking their parameters, which isn't very effective. We introduce the Cyclic Segmentation Generative Adversarial Network (CSGAN), a novel framework that produces high-quality manual annotations for unseen modalities by learning from annotated images in a different domain. By generating these annotations, CSGAN overcomes the primary limitation of using labeled data in traditional segmentation techniques. Our method was successfully evaluated using publicly available abdominal imaging datasets, and the results show that CSGAN can produce manual annotation-like masks for unseen modalities without the need for actual human annotations.

Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine
learning, including parameter sharing, Radial Basis Function kernels, and
adversarial training, to develop a novel RNN architecture for generating future
video features and anticipating actions. By using only the initial video frames and
a reduced number of parameters, Feature Mapping RNN efficiently generates future
frames and predicts actions, while its parameterization allows it to be trained
end-to-end in an action anticipation task. Our results show that Feature Mapping
RNN significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art action anticipation
models, including ours from earlier work, by a substantial 8.4% and 11.3% in
terms of mAP at early and late timestamps, respectively.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction method involves employing a machine learning algorithm to determine the flux at the observation's specific resolution, which is based on the modeling's comparison with chromospheric spectra. This prediction also accounts for an earlier empirical modeling of the flare's optical spectrum for a more accurate comparison with observations of the event. This revised model, which is based on an iterative process between observations and simulations, estimates near-UV continuum fluxes in agreement with data during the peak and late phases of the flare. However, a discrepancy remains between the model and data at the earliest stages of the flare, which may be attributed to an overestimation of the electron density in the model or an alternative energy release mechanism that could be responsible for the excess flux.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling a complete description of the deformation theory through the use of spinors and twisted Dirac operators. This research expresses the obstructions to finite-dimensional deformations in terms of a single elliptic operator applied to sections with specific properties. Additionally, we establish relationships between the deformation theory of G2-instantons and that of connections on principal bundles over three-dimensional simple Lie groups.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, the study targets p-core p'-partitions which adhere to these constraints. Notably, the largest of these p-core p'-partitions can be modeled by a long walk through a p-vertex graph, with edges assigned via the modulo p addition rule. Moreover, the research also identifies a systematic collection of significant p-core p'-partitions that establish a substantial lower limit on their maximum size.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the efficacy of TPC.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating ALOHA and CSMA protocols to minimize the impact of narrowband interference, introducing a new metric to gauge performance based on network throughput. In the case of ALOHA, we analyze the probabilities of interference and system efficiency under different system parameters. We observe that FMCW network behavior diverges from typical wireless communication patterns. In some scenarios, increased packet transmission can decrease interference probabilities. We introduce a clear channel assessment process, known as medium sensing, for CSMA, also defining metrics to gauge its effectiveness. In our analysis of CSMA, radar units transmit data after confirming an empty transmission path. We examine CSMA's medium sensing success rate, interference probabilities, and system efficiency under different system parameters. Unlike standard communication networks, the optimal strategy in some scenarios may involve the highest feasible attempt rates, contrary to conventional wisdom.

Recent experiments employing various methods have sought to detect the entangled two-photon absorption phenomenon across a range of materials. A new investigation adopts a distinct approach, focusing on analyzing changes in a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram resulting from entangled photon interaction. Utilizing Rhodamine B solution as a model nonlinear material exposed to 800 nm photons generated through type-II spontaneous parametric down conversion, researchers have discovered an unusual decrease in HOM interferogram visibility. Despite contradicting previous expectations, our findings reveal an unusual increase in spectral changes within the interferogram, offering insights into the entangled two-photon absorption process. By combining theoretical models with experimental data, this research provides crucial insights for identifying evidence of entangled two-photon absorption through analysis of spectral features and HOM interferograms.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform
state-of-the-art models using semantic matching on multiple evaluation metrics.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from this theory allows for the calculation of the acceleration of the ground surface in a precise and mathematically closed form, which can then be applied in various simulation methods to generate the sound waves. It is found that ground sound can be audible under certain circumstances in both realistic and highly idealized scenarios, contradicting previously held assumptions that ground sound cannot be perceived in realistic scenarios, and providing a new explanation for the phenomenon of perceived ground sound.

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without the use of inequalities. This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant research attention. Past studies on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have primarily involved perfect correlations from contextually exclusive measurements with accompanying certification strengths of at least $\frac{1}{2}$. Conversely, "sometimes-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have focused on non-perfect correlations. This paper aims to reverse the conventional distinction between "always-type" and "sometimes-type" all-versus-nothing proofs by establishing a "sometimes-type" proof relying on perfect correlations. This is accomplished through construction of a quantum state and measurement scenario of relevance, providing a non-locality certificate in the form of projective measurements on a bipartite system that yields outcomes of 1 or 0. Additionally, this paper clarifies the distinction between Bell nonlocality and Bell inequalities, solidifying the all-verses-nothing proof as a genuine manifestation of Bell nonlocality.

In flat band systems, constrained environments result in atypical behaviors influenced by randomness, indicating minimal movement. Molecular orbital representations of these systems introduce random MO models, retaining the degeneracy of the flat bands even in the presence of disorder. The zero modes in chiral systems with an imbalance in sublattices fall into this category. Following a general description of constructing flat bands through MOs, various examples are examined with numerical proof, including the sawtooth lattice in one dimension and the hyper-Pyrochlore lattice across any number of dimensions, extending the principles seen in two-dimensional Kagome and three-dimensional Pyrochlore lattices to higher dimensions.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and an abundance of hydrogen within its structure. Utilizing density functional theory, we've used first-principles calculations to investigate the electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties of this hydrogen boride. Surprisingly, our results show that the boron atoms in the sublattice participate sparingly in the phonon-mediated pairing process. Using the coherent potential approximation and Allen-Dynes models to evaluate superconducting properties, we've discovered that the sublattice with minimal hydrogen involvement strongly limits the material's superconducting critical temperature. Ultimately, our findings indicate that at most, a relatively low critical temperature of 5.1 K can be achieved in this hydrogen boride, significantly below its counterparts MgB2 and H3S.

Research on the division of quantities into equal parts continues to evolve. The findings presented here coincidentally relate to the numbers A124324 in the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences. A distinct counting method is developed for these numbers, and we establish a one-to-one correspondence between a specific type of division and the division of quantities into fewer equal parts. Furthermore, we introduce a set of numbers, $f_{n, k}$, which represent the count of a specific type of division containing $k$ distinct segments. Recursive relationships defining these numbers, along with their differential generating function, are provided. Identifying a closed form expression for these numbers is a desirable outcome. Lastly, we generalize our results to scenarios where the first segment consists of different parts, accompanied by combinatorial evidence.

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study the movement over the characteristics of the part of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, particularly demonstrating the rigidity where any stable movement is either comparable to a movement without characteristics or has a certain critical level. Notably, at higher levels of the characteristics, the movement becomes increasingly rigid, which is reflected in the groups becoming increasingly stiff. For instance, in the case of the group's stable part, at higher levels of the characteristics, its movement becomes nearly fixed, which is in line with a confirmed conjecture proposed by Serre and others.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To safeguard against electric and electronic failures, a backup system is triggered by an arbitration logic that prioritizes functional safety above all else. To uphold the standards set forth by ISO 26262, rigorous testing of this logic is mandatory. Through this validation, one can confidently ensure the reliability of system responses in times of crisis and prevent aberrant system states from materializing. Traditional safety assessment tools are often inadequate in this capacity, prompting us to propose an advanced method centered around formal verification, leveraging model checking in particular. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, we carefully recreate the driving system's dynamics, define and formalize key safety criteria, and scope the analysis within the guidelines specified by ISO 26262. Upon successfully verifying a high-automation fail-safe logic aligned with industrial standards, we discovered that current industrial practices are ultimately ineffective, uncovering critical shortcomings. To rectify this, we introduce an innovative architectural design, reinforcing fail-opportunistic modes and boosting the reliability of safety-critical system responses.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is essential for understanding phenomena and making predictions. Typically, researchers use pre-defined models or techniques that may not always yield the best results. In this study, we introduce a novel approach for clustering related systems using their dynamic properties. This method employs a data-driven framework that selects informative variables from multiple datasets and matches similar systems based on their trajectories. By leveraging the system dynamics, this approach can detect hierarchical and hidden patterns in the data. Furthermore, we develop a statistical tool to evaluate the results and provide accurate measures of the clustering structure. Experimental verification shows that this approach surpasses existing methods in accuracy and outperforms existing approaches in various applications.

Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called SPOT. This formalisation covers concepts such as the bounded/unbounded distinction, a distinction between quantities that are or are not assigned to points, a generalised equality relation applicable to quantities differing by negligible terms, and a continuity principle.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using data from interferometric HI intensity mapping surveys. Assuming that the galaxy density field is uniformly distributed on large scales, we derive analytical expressions for the bias factors governing the temperature and amplitude of the galaxy density field's power spectrum. Under the same assumption, we model the effects of foreground removal on these bias factors and estimate their magnitude based on existing data. We conduct a related analysis of the effects of foreground removal that allows the background signal to be modeled as a Gaussian random field with a given power spectrum. In addition to estimating the bias factors, we use perturbation theory to compute predictions for the band-averaged power spectra of the temperature and amplitude fields, which will be used to compare with actual data to constrain cosmological and astrophysical parameters in upcoming surveys.

Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers, then the sequence is linearly independent only when the dimension of the sequence's vector space is infinite. In our research, we derive this result as a specific instance of a more comprehensive model-theoretic finding. Then, focusing on vector spaces, we demonstrate that if a condition such as $T(e_i)=e_{\phi(i)}$ is to replace the previous operator assumption, $\phi$ must be equivalent to the successor function, defined as incrementing a number by 1. Finally, we explore a more complex generalization of this result, substituting the earlier operator assumption with a more complex condition.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document modeling have significantly improved accuracy by incorporating data like reviews, summaries, and narratives when user-item rating matrices are sparse. Nonetheless, these models are inadequate to learn optimal user and item representations. Collaborative filtering methods, including user-based and item-based, due to their efficiency and clarity, have been integrated with document-based methods to balance representation learning and recommendation quality. Our research improves upon existing hybrid methods by integrating context-aware document representation learning with behavior-based recommenders. Moreover, we refine and validate our solution with extensive experiments on real-world datasets.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. Moreover, we show the same spectral distribution's nth cumulant spectral measures converge towards a conditionally free convolution. These outcomes are equally true for other infinitesimally free families of matrices.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Attention is focused on isospin breaking and
the mixing between $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$, both of which are generated by meson-meson interactions. Our analysis indicates that the primary source of isospin breaking arises from transition matrix $T$ terms exhibiting isospin breaking and that additional isospin breaking arises due to the presence of loops containing kaons, as these do not cancel out when charged and neutral kaon masses differ. A calculated branching ratio for $a_0(980)$ production was found to be on the order of $5 \times 10^{-6}$. It is suggested that forthcoming experiments be conducted to investigate this problem, with the ultimate goal of better understanding scalar resonances through measurements of the $\pi^0 \eta$ mass distribution.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical capabilities to track multiple beams from the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI): a) a pupil tracker captures images of reference lasers using a two-dimensional CCD camera, b) a spatial filter aligns the telescope's pupil with the reference lasers, c) a beam tracker captures images of the science target and reference lasers using a two-dimensional CCD camera, and d) an optical delay unit maintains the phase difference between the science target and reference lasers. The camera's optical elements offer adjustable focus, zoom, and imaging capabilities to facilitate the assembly and testing of the GRAVITY instrument. The camera is composed of two identical modules that work in tandem to acquire images of the pupil and/or the target, or divide the science target's image into four sections to reconstruct the target's original format. The camera's optical elements have been characterized using various techniques, including measuring the modulation transfer function, assessing the resolution of captured images, and testing the movement of telescope actuators. This paper outlines the successful laboratory characterization of the GRAVITY acquisition camera components, presenting the measured parameters and explaining the associated testing procedures.

We investigate $k$-Center with a limited metric space, specifically seeking an optimal $f(n)$ value such that a given set of $n$ points with their distances not exceeding $\delta$, and a doubling or highway dimension, can be covered by $f(n)$ centers, placed at most $O(\delta)$ distance from the corresponding points. Our analysis indicates that $f(n)$ equals $2^{\Omega(\log n)}$ for doubling spaces and $f(n)$ equals $n^{\Omega(1)}$ for highway spaces, thus distinguishing between these two metric definitions and resolving an open question from Fruchterman's 1986 study on dimension reduction. This research also examines the $k$-Center problem under unique highway dimension and shows $k$-Center is NP-hard even for constant $k$ in this context.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1(x,y)(\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_2(x,y))=0$, where $m\in \mathbb{N}\cap \{k+1\}$, $Q_1(x,y)\in C^{\ell}( \mathbb{G})$, $Q_2(x,y)\in C^{k+\ell}( \mathbb{G})$, $\eta=(\eta_1,\eta_2)$ with $|\eta|=\sqrt{\eta_1^2+\eta_2^2}$, $\eta\not\equiv 0$, $\ell=0,1,2$, and $\mathbb{G}=\mathbb{C}^2$, is a constant.

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors, where the coefficients and variables of the system are defined over a finite field. Given a polynomial system with random errors of a specific bounded magnitude, we develop a probabilistic guarantee for a successful solution with a specified probability. Such a guarantee is the foundation for an efficient solver, which can take advantage of an optimal strategy to stop computations early and adapt to changing error patterns. Our theoretical findings, including a previously unknown bound for solving a polynomial system with bounded errors, have practical implications. Experiments using artificial data demonstrate the efficacy of this solver, which often yields a significantly faster solution time than a naive approach based on the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2$n$ correlations, and this emission's purity is improved due to the protective symmetry. Moreover, we illustrate the experimentally accessible nature of this phenomenon by applying it to a situation involving a pair of two-level systems coupled to a single cavity, which can model spin-orbit coupling or be implemented in a experiment using encircled dipoles or a double-quantum-dot-cavity system.

A unified analytical equation for the pressure of an equilibrium alkali metal plasma has been derived, which spans from a single component to a complex mixture of species. The derived equation incorporates contributions from ions in multiple states and includes a fundamental energy term that simplifies the calculation. The resulting expression for internal energy is a direct function of volume and temperature, which in turn enables the computation of other thermodynamic properties, such as energy, entropy, and Gibbs free energy. The developed model is versatile and can be applied to any component of group I in the periodic table, provided the necessary parameters for ionization and excitation are known. The accuracy of the model has been verified through numerous comparisons with numerical simulations and existing approximations, which also highlight the need and feasibility for future model improvements.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing a finite lowest-order local effective Lagrangian derived from QED for vector ρ and ω mesons, a mass spectrum as a function of momentum and chiral chemical potential is determined. Furthermore, in addition to the existing Chern-Simons effect, which differentiates between the transverse components of the mixed magnetic-electric field produced in the vector mesons, a new contribution arises due to the quasiparticle Fermi Dirac distribution of the medium's charged sector.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. Our work also involves establishing the impossibility of accurate size estimation in certain adverse conditions and, in the absence of malicious nodes, locates the computational efficiency limit for network size estimation, which poses a #P-hard problem.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a direct calculation instead of iterative methods. This technique is particularly efficient for scenarios with prominent conformal and vector dominant modes, reducing the computational time to a negligible fraction of the standard methods. However, it is now essential to monitor and correct any minor residual errors in these modes. This technique has been successfully implemented and tested with both single and multi-mode examples, including a study of a fundamental frequency and an initial data set resembling a collapsing black hole from Regge-Wheeler. The new method is anticipated to significantly enhance the performance of initial data generation in 3D simulations.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves identifying the neutrino mass ordering by utilizing a large, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector equipped with photomultiplier tubes. For optimal results, the experiment's instruments require precise energy resolution and quality, which necessitated a thorough assessment of the PMTs. Over four years, starting from 2017, a rigorous testing program for nearly 20,000 20-inch PMTs was carried out by the JUNO team. By examining these PMTs and implementing a series of stringent requirements, the experiment's investigators were able to verify the high quality of the selected instruments. This study outlines the thorough testing procedures used, the specifically designed testing equipment, and the statistical analysis of the 20-inch PMTs chosen for the experiment, covering over 15 performance indicators, including the uniformity of the photocathode. As a result, the largest batch of detailed-tested 20-inch PMTs ever produced, totaling 20,000 units from Northern Night Vision Technology Co. and Hamamatsu Photonics, was analyzed in the experiment.

In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. The complexity of multidimensional time series data presents significant model demands, necessitating models that can effectively capture long-term input interactions and compensate for noisy readings. Traditional multidimensional time series prediction models struggle to handle long-term causality, making them unsuitable for real-world applications. To address these challenges, a new framework using the Adaptive Graph Convolutional Network (ADGCN) is proposed. Combining an inherently flexible graph convolutional network with an adaptive sampling mechanism, the ADGCN framework enhances model capability to capture long-term input interactions and select key variables at different prediction horizons. By experimenting with the LSTF problem on real-world datasets from Brisbane and Melbourne, the proposed framework showcases its superiority over current models in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range using cross-dispersion spectrographs, which have an accuracy of 18 meters per arcsecond. By comparing various models in detail, we're now in a position to assess their suitability for different applications, such as operating modes that prioritize purity over resolution and vice versa.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data during the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform.

Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field near its Compton frequency, can be detectable even when its direct measurement is not sensitive enough to detect the signal directly due to its high frequency, because low-frequency fluctuations will occur as well due to its wave-like properties. A detector can therefore look for these low-frequency fluctuations, rather than just its high frequency oscillations, and is not limited to finding frequencies that are easily within its range, but can actually be searching for much larger and unexplored ranges of frequencies. A network of sensors, by cross-correlating their measurements, can detect these low-frequency fluctuations, and is not limited by bandwidth because low-frequency fluctuations will occur simultaneously at a range of frequencies. In this way, existing sensor networks can be used to experimentally explore the unexplored ranges of the parameter space of this bosonic dark matter.

This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The uniqueness and characteristics of BPC's solution rely on the eigenvalue properties of this matrix. The solutions range from a single, weighted Dirac mass for certain conditions to infinitely many Dirac masses in other cases. The number of Dirac masses in each case is influenced by the rank of a positive or negative semi-definite matrix. The positive or negative definiteness of the matrix also determines the weights of the Dirac masses as either nonnegative or nonpositive, respectively.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend, referred to as P4V1B, has been developed using the open-source compiler framework. In contrast to existing compiler backends, P4V1B demonstrates improved P416 program translation speed and reduced memory usage, outperforming commercial and open-source solutions in resource utilization efficiency. Furthermore, P4V1B accurately maps P416 programs to the specified architecture, achieving optimal results in benchmark programs, while providing flexible configuration options through programmable switches.

In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before performing the transport. This projection can be accomplished through various inner products, such as the $L^2$-projection or the "dirac" projection. Another approach utilizes a "weak" stability approach, temporarily introducing a pseudo-viscosity while another field, a charge, is being transported. Both methods were tested and validated using a range of benchmark tests and are currently being applied in simulations of freshwater and saltwater mixture dynamics.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results based on the Adult, Bank and Dutch datasets showcase the "interplay" between precision, equity, and confidentiality that occurs empirically as a direct outcome.

Scientists have discovered an excited state of the $B_c^+$ particle, which has a mass of approximately 6841.2 MeV. This state, which has a quadruplet spin structure, was found by analyzing proton-proton collisions from 2011 to 2012 using the LHCb detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. The $B_c^+(2S)$ state was found to have a mass that is 625.7 MeV higher than a previously reported state and 732.5 MeV higher than the $B_c^+(1S)$ state, which was previously identified. The newly found state was found to decay into $D^0\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$, with a relative branching fraction of $0.177 \pm 0.029 \pm 0.014$ compared to the $B_c^+(1S)$ state decaying into $D^0\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$. The study provides accurate measurements of two mass properties related to the $B_c^+$ particle, with a mass error margin of about 20 kiloelectronvolts and a $Q$-value error margin of about 17 kiloelectronvolts.

In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is analyzed where the non-dissipative boundaries initially deviate from Wada's characteristics, changing topologically. Focusing on the effects of dissipation, this study investigates how this system alters when weak dissipation lowers the system's energy below its critical value. Interestingly, this investigation finds that non-Wada basins transition into partially Wada basins under such weak dissipation. Moreover, numerical results demonstrate the emergence of Wada points on the boundaries of these basins in three-dimensional systems. Ultimately, this research indicates that Wada basins in three-dimensional systems exhibit increased stability when subjected to low levels of dissipation.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain "duration" window where the mass difference between two lepton types lies between their sum and the absolute difference. Although a moderately large interaction between this scalar field and the two lepton types could lead to extended lifetimes and larger observable distances between their birth and death points. By leveraging existing neutrino experiments and an upcoming one, we plan to explore various possible scenarios of this theoretical model. For instance, we can utilize data from the muonium decay rate and LSND production and decay patterns to evaluate this scalar's coupling, excluding the mass window indicated by the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly in the electron-muon sector. Furthermore, we analyze three major production processes at the muon tau collider, namely, muon and antimuon collision, muon collision with the antitau, and antimuon collision with the tau, to derive constraints on this scalar's coupling by considering both signal and background calculations.

Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
capacity for (1) extended temporal structure capture; (2) explicit modeling of 
temporal transitions between frames and segments, and (3) the ability to learn key 
regions in frames and temporal segments through its multi-step attention mechanism.
Evaluations of the model on established action recognition benchmarks indicate
remarkable performance superiority.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. The findings show that neither near-extremal nor extremal black holes can become overcharged due to the scattering. The outcome of scattering an equal amount of positive and negative charges is that the resulting state is a charged Reissner-Nordström black hole with less total charge, and therefore, the singularity in such black holes remains hidden behind the event horizon.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world dataset; and a scenario with a hidden variable.

We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex biological movement, addressing potential shortcomings in existing studies and providing new insights into its dynamics. Firstly, we address the issue of defining solutions for this model, highlighting inconsistencies in existing definitions. Secondly, we investigate the ability of solutions to produce branching trajectories. Lastly, we explore the possibility of extending existing results to consider multiple groups of moving entities.

Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The scenario presents a problem, particularly when these classifiers need to operate on low-resource devices or prevent performance overload on devices with IoT or industrial applications. A novel solution to overcome this challenge is proposed by NBcoded, a light attack classification tool that effectively combines noisy data removal and efficient data encoding, leveraging the benefits of Naive Bayes classifier while reducing resource requirements. In this study, three NBcoded implementations are developed using three Naive Bayes likelihood distribution assumptions (Gaussian, Complement, and Bernoulli). By comparing the results of the network intrusion detection dataset using 49 basic Naive Bayes classifiers and 49 NBcoded classifiers, the latter showed superior accuracy while requiring substantially less memory and processing time, an advantage that could be crucial for deploying cybersecurity classifiers on resource-constrained devices.

For finitely generated groups G, the focus of this article is the geometric property of growth in graphs representing faithful G-actions. We introduce a concept of Schreier growth gap, a function that measures group growth, by examining its implications on G's set actions. We then explore Schreier growth gaps for solvable groups. If G is metabelian and finitely presented or torsion-free, but not virtually abelian, it possesses a Schreier growth gap of n^2. If metabelian G has a Krull dimension of k, it will have a Schreier growth gap of n^k, such as the Schreier growth gap n^d for the wreath product C_p ∋¬ ℤ^d and n^(d+1) for ℤ ∋¬ ℤ^d. For solvable groups of finite Prüfer rank, a Schreier growth gap of exp(n) applies unless they are virtually nilpotent, a criterion which also applies to solvable groups linear over ℚ. Lastly, a wide range of torsion-free solvable groups have a Schreier growth gap of n^2, a group type that also includes those linear over ℚ.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as "biological locomotion" and distinguishes it from non-living objects to highlight its importance in environmental science, wildlife research, wildlife monitoring, pest control, agriculture, biomedical research and biomedical pest control. A distinguishing feature of biological creatures is that they often interact with other species, which requires distinguishing their movements from background activity. This document presents a method for automatically identifying moving biological creatures in video footage and differentiates them from stationary creatures, weather-induced movement, water movement, wind-induced movement, and other moving objects. A universal metric for measuring biological activity is proposed to automatically detect biological creatures in various environments in areas such as agriculture, forests, habitats, habitats near water, indoor environments, and wetlands. This metric is used to create automated detection tools for those applications. The document then describes other approaches to detecting biological creatures, which require manual labeling, and explains their advantages and limitations. A dataset called "Loconometry Benchmark" has been created with annotated footage of biological creatures, which includes creature sizes, shapes, and speeds, as well as information about backgrounds, backgrounds with other activity, weather-induced movement, water

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancies that inevitably arise. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the falling motions of objects with diverse size and mass, this work highlights several critical issues that need to be resolved by data-driven methods of automated physics discovery. It's particularly demonstrated that noise from measurements and secondary physical mechanisms such as complex drag forces, can mask the law of gravity, thus leading to incorrect model development. Utilizing the SINDy (sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics) method, which involves the use of real-world and simulated trajectory measurements, it's illustrated how the assumption that each object is governed by a similar physical law can increase the stability of learned models, although significant discrepancies between predictions and observations persist, primarily due to the intricacies of drag dynamics. This research shows that employing ML/AI in isolation will often be insufficient for accurately inferring universal physical laws and highlights the necessity for further modifications.

This study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the presence of hypothetical heavy, charged, long-lived particles in proton-proton collisions amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of data collected at 13 TeV energy. The search targets particles with significantly lower speeds than light and distinctive characteristics: substantial transverse momentum and unusually large energy loss per unit length. The study focuses on particles detectable by their tracks in the inner detector and energy loss measurements in the pixel layers of the detector, thus able to capture particles with lifetimes as short as one nanosecond and masses between 100 GeV and 3 TeV. The study explores the possibilities of long-lived particles in supersymmetric models, considering the production of $R$-hadrons, charginos and staus, with mass limits that extend well beyond previous search findings in various scenarios.

We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling efficiency in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot-cavity and a ridge waveguide by conducting simulations using the finite element method. A design optimized for a 1D nanobeam cavity yielded a notable source efficiency of 97.7 percent and an impressive Purcell factor of 38.6 for an isotropic dipole, primarily due to a combination of high index contrast between GaAs and SiO$_2$ materials and an effective cavity design that facilitated interference and minimized losses. However, we also identified mode mismatch as a limitation of our platform and proposed an optimization to improve efficiency further. Furthermore, our results demonstrated the importance of quantum dot alignment with the cavity's center for maximum extraction efficiency of both spatial and temporal modes.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that allows researchers to study dynamic properties and their connections to static structures, especially in disordered materials. This technique provides detailed information about the local and propagating modes in a dynamic structure function. Understanding the boson peak, a prominent feature in this function, is crucial as it is thought to be related to the terahertz-phonon overlap and represent a transition from propagating to localized modes. This chapter outlines recent advancements in identifying the boson peak using neutron scattering experiments, specifically focusing on its detection using different techniques and its relationship with material properties.

Particle physics is becoming a precise science driven by theoretical predictions, 
essential for analyzing experimental data. Future experiments like the LHC 
require advanced computations to understand single-particle properties and 
production processes. These calculations involve extremely complex equations, 
beyond current analytical methods' capabilities. This study proposes a 
semi-numerical technique using differential equations with specific boundaries 
at unique points to solve these complex equations with high accuracy. These 
calculations can be done using numerical methods like sector decomposition and 
are then translated into physical scenarios with a series of transformations, 
allowing for rapid evaluation with a high level of precision. This method has 
been successfully applied to complex calculations in QCD and electroweak theory, 
enabling the calculation of pole masses and decay rates with a high level of 
precision.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types.

Researchers have identified the far-side counterpart to a well-studied spiral arm in the center of the Milky Way, which is observed expanding. This far-side arm, detected through carbon monoxide emissions, can be followed in a map of Galactic longitude and velocity as a faint feature extending at least 20 degrees. Both the far-side and near-side arms exhibit comparable features including velocities, widths, heights, and mass distribution. Based on further investigation using 21-cm data, it's found that these spiral arms are primarily composed of molecular gas. This new evidence lends support to the presence of a bar structure at the center of the Galaxy and should aid in understanding its properties.

Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover a broad range of solutions. Our comparison across multi-objective optimization, multimodal optimization, and quality diversity in a straightforward context reveals that multi-objective optimization may not consistently generate significant diversity. By contrast, multimodal optimization tends to yield solutions with superior fitness levels. Meanwhile, quality diversity proves to be resilient to genetic neutrality and yields the most diverse set of solutions overall. Furthermore, integrating an autoencoder allows for the automated discovery of phenotypic features, which, in conjunction with quality diversity, facilitates the creation of a more extensive and diverse solution set. Ultimately, we offer strategic guidance on the appropriate applications of these optimization techniques.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. A variant of the Stable Roommates problem, incorporating additively separable preferences and including situations where rooms may have varying levels of desirability, is explored in this research. Unlike non-decreasing valuations, additively separable preferences present a more intricate case. A polynomial-time algorithm is proposed to solve this variant under the condition that rooms are equally desirable, resulting in full stability for instances where the size does not exceed four individuals. Conversely, it is demonstrated that finding optimal solutions for instances larger in scale becomes a computationally complex task. This particular variant represents a first documented instance of its kind, showcasing the complexity that arises from combining additively separable preferences with three-dimensional arrangements.

Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon
interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. When we
introduce structural irregularities, regional variations in strain have a
significant impact on valley behavior. We discovered that constant and
singly-humped electron-phonon interactions result in valley oscillations that
remain consistent, whereas a two-peaked mechanism leads to the total
elimination of these oscillations. In the presence of a confining potential,
valley oscillations are further exaggerated, and their dependence on quantum
states becomes highly variable, contingent on mechanisms of electron-phonon
interaction governing them. Moreover, novel mechanisms of electron-phonon
interaction may enable the spontaneous emergence of valley polarization in
two-dimensional materials.

We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing maximal subclasses within this group. Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor yields a transformed metric space, belonging to the same Gromov--Hausdorff class. This type of transformation can cause some clouds to jump into others, as observed, and we demonstrate that each cloud has a reference space, termed its core, such that transformations of this core space generate all clouds within the class. The core of a cloud is shown to be unique and consistant, consisting of a single metric space, whose distances are constant, called a minimax space, resulting from a specific limit of transformed distances. This core space, under certain conditions, is shown to be uniquely saturating, whose distances are consistently filled in the transformed limits.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components via top-layer microstrip coupling gap feed. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for the primary resonant frequency and inherently wide beamwidth for the second resonant frequency within the specified bandwidth, making this a highly efficient microstrip patch antenna for operation over a ground plane. The input impedance and radiation pattern observed through measured data closely agree with the simulated results.
