This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to +125{\deg}C operating range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C.

Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement can be generated by creating correlated states of light. However, in most cases, this entanglement is "mixed" and must be purified ("unscrambled") to exploit its full value. A major challenge lies in the fact that existing methods to extract entanglement typically require access to multiple identical quantum systems, which is often difficult to achieve. In contrast, quantum scissors provide a way to extract entanglement without this constraint by enabling the isolation of a single, entangled photon from others. In our experiment, we employ a hybrid combination of fiber and bulk optics for an integrated quantum system to develop an all-in-one approach for generating and isolating polarization entangled photons. This allows us to study the effects of noise on entanglement and sets the stage for its integration in future quantum devices.

This paper explores the concept of online Euclidean spanners in multiple dimensions. It considers the case where a sequence of points in R^d is given one at a time, and an algorithm must create and update a geometric t-spanner for each set of points as it arrives. Initially, the authors establish a lower bound of Ω(ε^(-1)log n / log ε^(-1)) for the competitive ratio of any online (1+ε)-spanner algorithm for points in 1-dimension, proving it to be tight. For sequences of points in R^d, the authors present algorithms under the L_2 norm that achieve competitive ratios of ε^(-2)log(ε^(-1)) / log(ε^(-1)) in constant dimension d ≥ 2, as well as ε^(-2) / log(ε^(-1)) in the worst-case scenario, independent of dimension. Our algorithms combine techniques from doubling covers, ball partitions, and online algorithms for convex hulls. Our results imply the existence of algorithms for finding tight worst-case spanners, and the tightest known worst-case (1+ε)-spanners in R^d are (1+ε)-approximations of a geometric t-spanner due to Swirepnek and Woechner.

Accurate categorization of IoT devices is a critical requirement, with implications extending to security and data protection aspects. Research has successfully applied machine learning methods for identifying IoT devices, with positive outcomes; yet current approaches disregard the costs involved in extracting device features from network data. This work presents a more practical viewpoint, contending that feature extraction comes with expenses varying across distinct features. Moving beyond existing research, this study investigates the impact of device features' costs on the multi-class classification process, formulating a framework that maximizes classification accuracy within a predetermined budget. The proposed model is grounded in support vector machines and is evaluated using real-world data from K-101 NetFlow, with experimental results illustrating its effectiveness in selecting suitable features for optimal performance.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with and without modal operators. These subvarieties correspond to axioms for three different extensions of classical and intutionistic modal logics, including the system BLM, its dual-contractive counterpart, and a version of the system with traditional contraction. The study presents Blair and Monzar types of algebras as primary ones, with the respective types of forest frames, including those for the traditional contraction system. The research is also extended to a multimodal version of the system with Knaster contraction, as well as a duality-theoretic interpretation of dual-contractive modal logic.

This research presents a novel and straightforward technique for word-alignment that leverages bilingual information from external sources like machine translation platforms. We demonstrate that a model with limited parameters can achieve performance comparable to GIZA++ when trained on a relatively small dataset. Furthermore, in terms of alignment metrics, such as accuracy or F-score, our approach delivers results equivalent to GIZA++ when trained on a dataset 22 times smaller. Crucially, the method's domain-agnostic training capabilities enable 'on-the-fly' application on any new pair of sentences without requiring extensive retraining.

We suggest an asynchronous algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium problems by iteratively decomposing the mixed strategies. This methodology is heavily grounded in monotone operator theory, utilizing warped resolvents for handling a combination of nonsmooth and smooth functions involved in strategy mixtures.

This research delves into the realm of Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) forming a significant portion of Dark Matter (DM), with a focus on their potential influence on cosmic structure formation through gravitational effects. Despite the lack of direct PBH detection, they remain a valid hypothesis to explain DM, with constraints imposed by various observational evidence, such as the duration of the cosmic microwave background's (CMB) reionization period and the absence of excess gamma-ray signals from nearby galaxies. If PBHs make up DM, they must reside within a specific mass range, with gravitationally influenced dark matter as a viable alternative to the standard dark matter model. To investigate this, we employ the PopSyCLE code to conduct N-body simulations mapping the movement of dark matter halos for three distinct PBH mass range scenarios. Our simulation results include the prediction of detectable levels of secondary mercurial plasma signals in the GW spectrum and measurable distortions in the CMB, along with an analysis of the distribution of dark matter and subhalo abundance within each PBH mass range scenario.

In a system where rigid wedge-shaped objects are placed in a narrow channel,
multiple types of ordered phases occur, which vary depending on the overall shape of the wedge,
the width of the channel, and the number of objects placed within it.
When these wedge-shaped objects are made up of spheres, as seen in our research, a
particular type of ordered phase shows a specific tension pattern and aligns
spatially in a uniform manner within the channel.
Based on our findings, in the case of isotropic objects, only two types of ordered phases
exist: a parallel arrangement with no tension and a staggered arrangement with alternating
tensions.
However, when the shape of the object becomes asymmetric, a spiral arrangement with a uniform
tension pattern emerges in the ordered phase.
Additionally, our research found that in the spiral arrangement, all system components exhibit
symmetric rotation.
We also discovered through our research that in the system with asymmetric objects, three types of
ordered phases with uniform tensions exist: a staggered, oblique, and spiral arrangement.
Our research provides a diagram that outlines these different phases and can be applied to systems
where rigid objects are placed in narrow channels.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness.

A conventional imaging scenario hinges on three essential elements: a light source that illuminates and scatters off the subject of interest; a means to detect this scattered light; and a detector that can resolve spatial information. However, the typical ingredients of imaging may be insufficient for delicate biological specimens or sensitive samples due to the inadequacy of available light sources and detection capabilities. Nevertheless, we devise and execute a quantum imaging protocol that adapts to challenging situations by substituting the conventional imaging approach with a novel, single-pixel measurement procedure. This innovative method employs a Mach-Zehnder interferometer and relies on interaction-free measurement to circumvent the limitation of detecting scattered light. Instead, it utilizes undetected photons and relies on a quantum measurement outcome to reconstruct the image of the hidden object. This technique offers the advantage of requiring no light source and no ability to resolve fine details, yet still yields an image of the object. Furthermore, we note that, although the protocol does not involve a light source, a coherent state is used to prepare the input quantum field.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements, visual observations, and simulations, we investigate the impact of roughness on liquid foams during motion. The results reveal the occurrence of friction enhancement due to roughness, rather than a decrease as might be expected. The phenomenon is attributed to two main factors: the distribution of liquid polyhedra at the interface affected by roughness and the presence of surface asperities that hinder motion. The complexity of roughness surfaces introduces a wide range of stresses during flow, leading to a'stress diversity' effect that amplifies the frictional force. Additionally, the distribution of polyhedra gives rise to 'jamming' states, where increased stress is required for further movement, resulting in elevated frictional resistance. The influence of surface roughness on liquid foams also exhibits'memory effects,' where the history of the surface roughness is recorded and affects the stress, even when the roughness is no longer in contact with the liquid. The'stress diversity' and'surface history' effects are quintessential manifestations of the unique interactions between surface roughness and complex liquids.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a decision tree-based classification system for cancers and lesions, and analyzed metadata to identify atypical images. A two-stage process was devised to handle the anomalous image issue, involving image classification and outlier detection. To enhance our model's performance, we introduced a pre-training step using 50,000 synthetic training images. The integration of entropy into our model enabled us to accurately identify the anomalous image class.

We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement of its electronic mass is slightly less than expected from earlier research. These findings amplify the need for theoretical models more advanced than the random phase approximation. Contrary to the hypothesis suggesting significant acceleration of the carriers due to their interaction with spin fluctuations, our results do not support this theory. Additionally, a comparison with previous electron loss data indicates that sodium's mass enhancement due to dipole-type electron-hole interactions is substantially less than its mass enhancement due to monopole-type interactions measured using ARPES.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its nonnegative value during free expansion, which holds surprising implications.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on globalization. We'll demonstrate how curvature graph weights can be explicitly defined through a hypergeometric function and an even simpler expression that combines it with a formula for the underlying connection graph weights. Notably, we examine a cotangent bundle case, leading to a substantial simplification of the curvature expression.

We explore solitary waves known as "nanoptera," characterized by exponentially small oscillations, in precompressed woodpile and diatomic granular chains. These solitary waves emerge from the Stokes phenomenon as special curves in the complex plane are intersected. Additionally, we investigate the hydrodynamic approximation and confirm that solitary waves without oscillations occur, marking a departure from the case of compression by shear.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we look at any sharp feature within an inflationary model. These features can induce unsuppressed quantum fluctuations in heavy fields, leaving detectable signatures in primordial non-Gaussian patterns, which are investigatable in future studies of primordial features.

Consider a graph of even order G and its complete graph counterpart K_G. A pairing of G refers to a perfect matching of K_G. A graph has the PH-property if for each pairing of K_G, it shares a perfect matching that, when combined, creates a Hamiltonian cycle of K_G. Cubic graphs that possess the PH-property have been fully characterized by Alahmadi et al. in 2015, and it follows logically that quartic graphs should be the subject of characterization next. In our work, a class of quartic graphs called accordion graphs is defined, parameterized by n and k, which we designate as A[n,k]. We find that a specified family of infinite quartic (also circulant) graphs that possess the PH-property belong to the general class of accordion graphs. The paper delves into the properties of accordion graphs in terms of pairings, which sometimes coincide with perfect matchings of G, and examines their close relationship with the Cartesian product of two cycles. Recent findings by Bogdanowicz have prompted a complete characterization of accordion graphs as the quartic graphs possessing the PH-property. In particular, it is proven that A[6k,2] is non-empty for all k values.

We carry out a finite-time scaling analysis near the detrapping point in a three-state quantum walk model. The coin operator is adjusted using parameter $\rho$ that controls the speed of wavepacket dispersion. The initial state is a symmetric superposition of two coin operator eigenstates with mixing angle $\theta$. One eigenstate corresponds to full wavepacket spreading at $\theta_c(\rho)$ where none of the wavepacket remains near the initial position. At the detrapping angle, key metrics such as survival probability and participation ratio exhibit one-parameter scaling behavior. Moreover, we demonstrate that the participation ratio grows with time, specifically in a logarithmic-corrected linear fashion, thereby resolving reported sublinear tendencies.

This paper explores the benefits that self-supervised learning confers on Vision Transformer (ViT), distinguishing it from convolutional networks (convnets). Our findings show that self-supervised ViT features uniquely capture the semantic structure of an image, unlike supervised ViT, which we find resembles an ensemble of convolutional networks. Furthermore, we observe that the learned features from self-supervised ViT are proficient in visual recognition and can be utilized for attribute-based image retrieval. Our analysis indicates that the ViT's sensitivity to raw image pixels contributes to its ability to learn semantically structured features. Moreover, we introduce the concept of 'emerging structure,' which refers to the organized patterns of features that emerge from self-supervised ViT, distinct from random ViT.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the dissipative effect in this model. Using a phase space analysis in conjunction with Hubble data, the model's equations of state have been constrained during the model's evolution. As a result, the model undergoes a transition from dark energy-like behavior in the early stages to dark matter-like behavior in the latter stages, exhibiting non-phantom, and ultimately, matter-dominated behavior in its later stages.

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li.

Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet achieving high-quality results typically requires multiple iterations. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, restricting artist control. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Stable Artist, an image editing technique allowing artists to exert precise control over the image generation process. Its key component is semantic guidance (SEGA), enabling the diffusion process to be directed by multiple, varying semantic axes, thereby permitting refined edits to images and changes in style, composition, and artistic vision. Furthermore, SEGA facilitates the exploration of latent spaces, providing insights into the complex concepts, like 'carbon emission,' learned by the model. We illustrate the Stable Artist's capabilities through various demonstrations, showcasing its ability to create stunning, high-resolution images.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in more precise steganographic data extraction compared to the conventional approach based on predictive uncertainty quantification.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter in certain effective field theories imposes the most stringent limits on energy scales compared to theories describing visible photon spectra. Additionally, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can significantly constrain valid parameter spaces in neutrino and dark matter scenarios, particularly when the energy scales initially appear to be heavily restricted. For example, in the case of neutrinos with mass arrangements less than the J/ψ mass, J/ψ invisible decays can still allow energy scales up to 5 GeV, whereas direct invisible decays can only accommodate scales below 1.5 GeV. Similarly, for dark matter with mass arrangements less than the J/ψ mass, J/ψ invisible dec

High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere reveal tiny magnetic bright points, associated with extremely strong magnetic fields, present throughout the solar cycle. These features, extensively detected in Ca II photospheric layer, appear as minute, scattered points, highly active in motion, and exhibit distinct behaviors depending on the solar phase. To gain insight into their structure and development, researchers investigated the size, shape, and distribution of these features in the solar photosphere using advanced tracking techniques and a specialized analysis method. By applying a cumulative distribution function to observe the size of these bright points, researchers found evidence of a biphasic distribution, consistent with earlier findings of distinct groups of these features, and provided quantitative support for this classification. The size of the smaller group, consisting of highly active magnetic regions, aligns with theoretical predictions, while the larger group, consisting of quieter magnetic regions, presents a puzzling size discrepancy. The size of the quieter magnetic regions was found to be substantially larger than expected, even in the solar maximum, suggesting the possibility of magnetic field depolarization due to strong local gradients. Researchers also discovered distinct distributions of the area and diameter of these features, and the respective ratios, providing further evidence of the complex nature of these solar phenomena.

Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear. This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in scenarios where individual sources are insufficient. Researchers achieved this insight by analyzing'minimal videos' - brief clips that facilitate reliable object, part, and action recognition, but are unrecognizable when spatial or temporal constraints are compromised. Unlike existing deep networks, humans exhibit more adept performance in these complex configurations, highlighting missing dynamic vision mechanisms in current models.

Dark particles interacting through Abelian gauge symmetries and ordinary matter through kinetic mixing result in the manifestation of broken $U(1)$ magnetic monopoles in our observable universe as milli-magnetically charged entities confined to laboratory scales. However, they possess an unconfined "electric" charge equivalent to several thousands, given that the monopole and antimonopole pair production via processes like pair production and dark bremsstrahlung falls short of the current limits set by MiniBoone and future experiments by at least three orders of magnitude. As a consequence, these dark monopoles remain unconfined and freely move through laboratory and astrophysical environments. We explore the impact of these interactions on the galactic magnetic field and magnetic fields within the intracluster medium. Additionally, we investigate the effect of dark monopole-induced friction on the galactic rotation curve and the potential constraints on this scenario by analyzing data from the observed galactic rotation curve.

The rapidly evolving Earth Observatory research area has immense potential to utilize AI in real-time weather forecasting. This work addresses the challenge of accurate weather prediction by leveraging the video transformer network. Building on existing research into vision transformer architectures, we address the limitations associated with their high computational complexity and data-hungry nature. To achieve this, we propose combining Video Swin-Transformer with a dedicated data generator, ensuring compatibility with limited dataset resources. Furthermore, we introduce the Spatial-Temporal Cross-Attention module to replace the standard multi-head attention mechanism, thus reducing computation complexity. The Video Swin-Transformer network equipped with the proposed STCA module is then applied to the weather forecasting task in the Boston area. Experimental results demonstrate that the enhanced network outperforms baseline models, showcasing its effectiveness and efficiency in weather prediction.

In models that expand on the electroweak sector, a basis can be found where the symmetry prevents coupling, leading to viable 'invisible' dark matter candidates. We investigate the stability of states in low-scale three Higgs doublet models with $S_3$ symmetry, where the basis' lack of connection to physical observables makes predictions difficult. However, we find that with a perturbation allowing Higgs mixing, a dark matter candidate can emerge, and this scenario is consistent with current particle and cosmic density constraints. Two potential dark matter candidates emerge in this theoretical framework: a naturally occurring stable state and another that can be made long-lived through selection rules.

A comprehensive study on the PPT square conjecture is presented with a notable achievement: the PPT square conjecture's validity has been rigorously demonstrated for the case involving finite-dimensional space.

Intracellular transportation is crucial for delivering vital substances to complex branched neural networks, enabling their survival and operation. Disruption of this process is associated with various neurodegenerative diseases, making it vital to understand how neurons control transportation to target essential areas. We introduce a new optimization model that simulates the material transportation mechanism in complex neural topologies. The model adheres to partial differential equations that align with experimental evidence and is validated through comparison with real neuroimaging data. By solving this equation set through a sequential least squares method, we generate solutions that predict material flow in complex neural architectures. Unlike existing models, our approach accounts for material accumulation through a nonlinear regulation term, facilitating quantitative comparisons between model predictions and experimental measurements.

Billion-dollar losses inflicted by banking fraud each year underscore the need for effective anti-fraud tools. To address this, researchers have developed the Node-Weighted Network motifs detection (NeMo) method, which can identify regular patterns in a network, like irregular transaction sequences. This study presents two evaluation strategies for NeMo: a simulated environment for testing its accuracy and a real-world validation using a dataset of actual banking transactions. The goal is to determine the optimal parameter settings that balance precision and computational efficiency.

In a black hole-white dwarf binary system, we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a portion of its mass, causing the black hole to experience an influx of matter. This mass accretion leads to the generation of intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, echoing patterns observed in recently discovered X-ray sources. The energy emitted from the accretion process initially manifests as brief, high-frequency bursts at each close approach, but eventually, the surrounding disc becomes a sustained source of radiation, emitting electromagnetic and gravitational waves in a continuous pattern.

Three-body $\tau$-decays, which involve semileptonic interactions with light hadrons and CP symmetry violations, can provide insight into these processes. Studies of weak electromagnetic interactions rely on form factors to describe the hadronic part of the final states, which can be further understood by decomposing the hadronic current into specific orbital angular momentum components. Given the increasing data availability from future experiments, a new description of the hadronic currents is presented in terms of the quantum numbers of the final hadronic state using the isobar model. Additionally, the work includes formulas for orbital angular momenta and the rules for describing the decay chains of arbitrary mass hadronic three-body systems, which also improves existing descriptions in terms of form factors.

Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky ratio models" with parameters $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ where $\alpha$ ranges between $0$ and $1$ and $\beta$ is greater than $0$. The inverse of each $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ function, denoted as $D_{\alpha,\beta}$, represents a semimetric for all possible subsets of a given set. Our research found that the function $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ is indeed a metric if $\alpha$ lies within the interval from $0$ to $0.5$ and $\beta$ is greater than or equal to $1/(1-\alpha)$. The verification of this outcome was achieved through an exhaustive proof by induction. The particular cases of $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ occur when it equals the Jaccard distance when $\alpha$ is $0.5$ and it also resembles the normalized normalized information distance when both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ equal $1$. Moreover, our research established that $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ is compatible with any of the monotonicity properties it possesses, provided that $\alpha$ is less than or equal to $0.5$ and $\beta$ is greater than or equal to $1/(1-\alpha)$.

Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired synthetic data for training frameworks, aiming to directly convert blurry inputs to clear outputs. However, the success of these methods heavily relies on high-quality synthetic blurry data available only before training, a constraint that becomes impractical with large datasets. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an on-the-fly data augmentation technique to create blurry inputs dynamically during training and testing. To make the most of this approach, we adopt an unconventional framework incorporating a sequential process of blur removal and subsequent reblurring with the assistance of a module that mimics real-world blur, as well as hand-crafted prior knowledge based on advanced statistical human body models. This module not only enhances the deblurring algorithm's ability to distinguish between human and non-human regions but also improves overall outcomes compared to other recent state-of-the-art methods through adversarial learning.

Hebbian theory aims to explain how brain cells modify their responses to stimuli, ultimately leading to the ability to learn. A notable aspect of Hebbian learning is its ability to occur independently, without requiring external feedback. This concept is further explored in a research paper, which outlines a novel, chemical-based system capable of exhibiting autonomous Hebbian learning through multiple input channels. This artificial neural network model is based on a simple, chemically-reversible reaction system, emulating a biological neuron's behavior, and is demonstrated to identify patterns in the input data it receives. In addition to the fundamental reaction system, the researchers propose more complex variations that incorporate enzymes and compartmentalised reactions to simulate biological systems, as well as a DNA-based system built upon the principle of DNA strand displacement. These innovative models offer promising avenues for exploring autonomous learning and potentially developing biological intelligent systems.

The ultrapower of any ordered set is created as a refined version of the set itself by taking into account infinite sequences of elements from it. This process involves dividing the sequences into classes according to a set of rules defined by an ultrafilter, leading to a set that always satisfies a fundamental property of ordered sets. It turns out that a set's openness determines its ability to fulfill the open completeness property in the refined version, whereas its original cardinality dictates whether the refined version is complete.

Scientific breakthroughs in data-driven science increasingly rely on applying sophisticated AI models to comprehensive, discipline-specific datasets. However, the computational resources required to evaluate every possible model against a full dataset prove impractically expensive, leading researchers to omit certain models or reduce the available data for testing purposes. These limitations impede the advancement of reliable model selection, thereby jeopardizing the credibility of the scientific findings that rely on such models. In this study, we investigate the potential of data-specific profiling as a more realistic approach to facilitating model selection, by rapidly identifying subsets of a large dataset that effectively represent the original data and can be used to accurately evaluate models against it. We assess the efficiency and accuracy of two distinct profiling techniques - one based on random sampling and the other on balanced clustering - using three scientific datasets from different fields: astronomy, biology, and climate science. Our results demonstrate that both techniques can generate subsets that reproduce the original results with a high degree of accuracy, at varying levels of computational expense. We discuss how the choice of profiling technique depends on specific research priorities and available resources, offering a practical solution to the long-standing problem of model selection.

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with t colors includes a complete graph with t vertices. This has been reinforced by another theory suggesting if a given graph is assigned t colors, where a certain set of its vertices uses every possible color, then that graph must have a complete graph with t vertices within it. This more robust idea has been tested with success for the case of t = 4. This result holds further implications for 5-colored graphs; specifically, we can confirm a revised and more robust version of the original Hadwiger's conjecture, where 5-colored graphs contain complete graphs with 5 vertices within them. This has further implications for 5-critical graphs in the same scenario.

This research introduces an advanced algorithm for efficiently recovering smooth graph signals through generalized correntropy, and a specific loss function is formulated accordingly. Derived from the aforementioned principle, the algorithm is developed further, and a variant leveraging kernel width adaptation is presented. Results indicate that this adaptive kernel width variant surpasses the fixed kernel approach. In addition, the research undertakes theoretical examinations of the algorithm's properties. Firstly, the analysis focuses on proving the cost function's convexity. Secondly, the stability of the algorithm is analyzed under uniform conditions. Lastly, the mean convergence of the algorithm is assessed. Furthermore, the computational complexity of the algorithm is analyzed. Experiments conducted using synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the superiority of the proposed algorithm over existing methods for adaptive graph signal recovery.

Theoretical investigations are conducted to design and control entangled atomic states formed through spin-changing collisions within a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate for use in a more robust atom interferometry capable of withstanding common technical problems like detector limitations. It is discovered through both analytical and numerical examinations of the spin-changing collision process that utilizing a small initial disturbance as a trigger, as opposed to vacuum fluctuations, yields superior results despite reduced entanglement. Our findings have implications for optimizing entangled atomic state production for quantum-enhanced matter-wave interferometry applications.

The purpose of this research paper is to derive optimal estimates for the first eigenvalue of the first Robin eigenvalue problem involving the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator. This problem seeks to minimize a specific functional over all nonzero functions in the Sobolev space, and involves several variables and constants, including $p$, a bounded mean convex domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, and a smooth boundary smooth function $\gamma$. We discovered new lower and upper bounds for this eigenvalue problem based on the first eigenvalue of a one-dimensional nonlinear problem. Specifically, for positive $\lambda$ we proved a lower bound for the eigenvalue and conducted numerical analysis to estimate the difference between the eigenvalue and the one-dimensional value. Furthermore, we proved upper and lower bounds for the eigenvalue in terms of the anisotropic inradius of $\Omega$ and the parameter $\gamma$.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity for processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process.

A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance. Specifically, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm integrates external sequence models, derived from the parser's application to unlabelled data, into the parser using a sophisticated weighting system. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted across multiple languages in diverse settings, and the results clearly indicate that our approach outperforms traditional self-training and state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods by a significant margin.

Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-trivial, invertible-defying symmetries. By utilizing holographic duality, we can determine the branes equivalent to these symmetries, and deduce the fusion principles for the symmetries through brane dynamics.

Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) stands out as the most promising approach to tackle decision problems within PTIME (polynomial time) complexity, having demonstrated the capability to be contained within PTIME and yet unseparated from it. A prominent challenge lies in resolving the isomorphism problem for unordered Cai-Furer-Immerman graphs, known as the CFI-query, which has remained undefined within CPT despite being classified as a PTIME decision problem. A significant development has been achieved in underscoring that the partial equivalence problem for pairs of polynomial circuits possesses profound implications, as it has the ability to implicitly define a solver for the CFI-query problem. This implicit solver would rely on a reduction by an amount equivalent to the circuits' description size, a reduction threshold that poses a question - is the CFI-query decidable through a polynomial description? This inquiry is in line with current CPT research hypotheses. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the partial equivalence problem for pairs of polynomial circuits can be expressed through a symmetric circuit class, referred to as SCPT, which is an extension of CPT with symmetric access. This implicit SCPT solver would also facilitate a reduced description size, thereby providing potential insights into its decidability in relation to CPT.

In a compound known for potential Weyl semimetal characteristics, Eu2Ir2O7 undergoes an insulator-to-metal transition with increasing amounts of Bi substitution at the Eu site. To explore the properties of the resulting series, Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7 was studied via HAXPES. Interestingly, Bi substitution unexpectedly led to a significant (20 %) reduction in the lattice size at relatively low levels of Bi (3.5 %) doping. The experiments using HAXPES showed that the ions retained their intended valence states across the entire range of the series. The observed variation in Bi core-level spectra among metallic compositions implies that the Bi ions participate in the formation of the Fermi energy's density of states. The valence band density functional theory and HAXPES data were then compared to confirm consistency between theoretical predictions of the material's properties and the experimental results of the Bi valence state.

Consider a metric space ${\mathfrak M}=({\mathcal M},\rho)$ and a Banach space $X$, with a set-valued mapping $F$ that maps ${\mathcal M}$ to the power set of $X$, and is defined as ${\mathcal C}={\mathcal C}(F)$, and denoted as a subset of $X$. The core of $F$, often referred to as a set of regular elements, is defined as ${\mathcal C}_\varepsilon^r(F)$ with a corresponding definition for its truncated version ${\mathcal C}_\varepsilon^b(F)$. For a low dimensional set-valued mapping where the dimension is no higher than 2, and is Lipschitz, it has been proven that its core exists under specified conditions which include Lipschitz continuity, and when $F$ is upper semi-continuous, a distinct set of conditions applies. A distinct approach is required for its truncated version. The existence of ${\mathcal C}_\varepsilon^{br}(F)$ can also be determined using an alternative method. The core of a monotone mapping, as well as a mapping with compact images, can be shown to exist without reliance on extra conditions.
